summary:
Copula clauses are a subtype of non-verbal predication and are described separately because the copula has several idiosyncratic properties. It lacks a restricted stem, has different non-dual and dual stems (rä vs. rn), and shows irregular third-person singular non-past inflection; its stem rä can also occur in an ambifixing template meaning ‘do’.  

Copula clauses take a copula subject and complement and can express identity between two noun phrases or be used in presentational constructions. The complement may also appear in proprietive or privative case to indicate existence or non-existence, and adjectives or property nouns can function as copula complements as well.

text:
In terms of verb morphology, intransitive clauses have been described in morphologicaltemplates. The verb inflection employs the prefixing or the middle template. Their single argument is always in the absolutive case. Two examples are given in ( ex562 ) and ( ex563 ).

The two prefixing verbs in ( ex562 ) have no overt subject noun phrases, but the second clause contains an adjunct marked with the purposive case karr `for a village' (or settlement place). In example ( ex563 ), we see the middle verb brigsi `return' and the subject pronoun nzä in the absolutive case.

exe
ŋarsenzo swanyakm... karr swanrenzrm.\\
ŋars=en=nzo swan yakm (.) kar=r swan renzrm\\
river= =.:::: /walk (.) village=.:::: /look.around\\
`He was coming along the river... he was looking for a place to settle.'\\ tci20120922-09DAK #14-15

exe
exe
nzä boba fthé kanathrfa zänbrima.\\
nzä boba fthé kanathr=fa zän brima\\.. when kanathr=:::: /return\\
`That was when I returned from Kanathr.' tci20120805-01ABB #607

exe
summary: Intransitive clauses are described with verb inflection that uses either the prefixing or the middle template, and their single argument is always in the absolutive case. The examples show prefixing verbs without overt subject noun phrases, with one clause containing a purposive adjunct, and a middle verb where the subject pronoun appears in the absolutive case.

text:
Impersonal clauses are expressed using the middle template of the verb, in which a person-invariant middle marker fills the prefix slot, while the suffix indexes the single argument of the predicate ( middletemplatesubsection ). The indexed noun phrase, if present at all, occurs in the absolutive case. The salient feature of this clause type is that the referent of the verb indexing is impersonal, unclear or simply empty. Consider examples ( ex737 ) and ( ex738 ). In the first example, the speaker talks about rain-making magic, which involves a rotting mixture of meat and honey in bottles. These bottles or containers are opened and the rising odour is said to increase the rainfall. The third singular indexed by the verb form kfäkor refers to the changed weather conditions, and the English translation `it was enough' exhibits the same general or impersonal meaning. The second example contains the noun aki `moon', but it is unclear whether the verb really indexes this noun or whether its referent is empty. Hence, the two possible translations. During the transcription of example ( ex738 ), the first translation was the preferred one in this particular context.

exe
watikthénzo fthé kfäkor... we sgu thwäthbe woz thwärmäne.
watik-thé=nzo fthé kfä kor (.) we sgu thwä thbe woz thwä rmäne\\
enough- = when:: /become (.) also plug: >:: /put.inside bottle: >:: /close\\
`When it was enough, we put the lids back in and we closed the bottles.'\\ tci20110810-01MAB #59-62

exe
exe
aki zbo kräkor. \\
aki zbo krä kor\\
moon.::: /become\\
`It became moon(light) here.' or `The moon came up here.' tci20120904-02MAB #47

exe

Example ( ex557 ) is a description of a picture as part of a stimulus task. The speaker takes on the role of a man in the picture and asks: `What is going on?'. Again, the verb form krewär appears in the middle construction and indexes a third singular.

exe
sinzo foba ynrä nima ``ra krewär bobo?'' \\
si=nzo foba yn rä nima ra kre wär bobo\\
eye=..:::: /be what::: /happen. \\
`He was just looking from over there and wondered: ``What is going on there?''' tci20111004RMA #353

exe

Impersonal constructions often involve light verbs, for example rä- `do' and ko- `become', which take a nominal predicate, for example a noun or property noun. In these cases, the nominal predicate will be unmarked for case, like the absolutive case. Therefore, it may be difficult to decide whether (i) it is a nominal predicate and the subject is empty, or (ii) whether the noun phrase in question is the subject indexed in the verb. Consider example ( ex559 ), in which the speaker describes the location of the mythical place of origin Kwafar, which is located in the Arafura sea between Papua New Guinea and Australia. The verb form ŋakonzr `it becomes' occurs in the relative clause, which is printed in boldface. The third singular indexed in the verb form could be mazo `ocean' (lit. `where the ocean becomes') or it could be an empty subject (lit. `it becomes ocean').

exe
thden rera... zane zena mane bad mane wythk mazo mä ŋakonzr a... australiane bad mä wythk.\\
thd=en rära (.) zane zena mane bad mane w ythk mazo mä ŋa konzr a (.) australia=ane bad mä w ythk\\
middle=Loc.::: /be (.): today which ground which.::: /come.to.end and (.) australia= ground where.::: /come.to.end\\
`It was in the middle... this one, where the land ends... where it becomes ocean until where Australia's land ends.' tci20131013-01ABB #26-30

exe

Weather events often have empty or impersonal subjects. This can be shown with prefixing verbs as well as middle verbs. A common way to say `It is going to rain' is shown in ( ex739 ). It is clear that nor `for rain' is not indexed in the verb because it is flagged with a non-core case, the purposive case. Therefore, the reference of the third singular in the verb form is empty.

exe
nor yé. \\
no=r yé\\
rain=.::: /be\\
`It will rain.' (lit. `It is for rain') 1pt [overheard]

exe

Another example is the phrase wär kwan yanor `it is thundering' in ( ex740 ). The thunder is expressed by the ideophone wär kwan `thundering noise', and all ideophones of this type are nominal compounds headed by kwan `noise, sound' ( ideophones-sec ). The verb yannor is inflected for a masculine subject, but kwan is feminine. Hence wär kwan is not the subject, and a literal translation would be: `He shouts the thunder sound'. Again the reference of `he' is empty.

exe
wär kwan yanor. \\
wär kwan ya nor\\
thunder.::: /shout\\
`It is thundering.' 1pt [overheard]

exe

Other weather or sound phenomena can be expressed by verbs in the middle template. In example ( ex558 ), the verb `start' is inflected for a subject, but its referent is unclear partly because the verb does not index an object. Thus, the indexed argument could be (i) the sound of the fire (`The fire sound started'), or (ii) it could be an empty subject (`It started the fire sound').

exe
fi mni zürnane u kwan zethkäfako. \\
fi mni zürn=ane u kwan ze thkäfako\\
but fire smoke=. roaring.sound:::: /start\\
`but the fire smoke's sound started (rumbling).' tci20120827-03KUT #186-187

exe
summary: Impersonal clauses in this language use the middle verb template, with a person-invariant middle marker in prefix position and suffixes that index a single argument, usually in the absolutive case. However, the referent indexed by the verb may be empty, unclear, or impersonal, especially in clauses describing weather, sound, or other events. Examples with verbs like “become,” “do,” “rain,” and “thunder” show that it is often difficult to tell whether an overt noun phrase is the indexed subject or a nominal predicate with an empty subject.

text:
Passives meanings are expressed in two ways: (i) by a verb in the middle template which indexes a patient role; the indexed noun phrase occurs in the absolutive case ( middletemplatesubsection ), or (ii) by a resultative construction, in which a nominalised verb is flagged with the instrumental case ( inscase ). Note that both are not dedicated passive constructions. Instead, they should be understood as constructions which can express passive-like semantics.

Example ( ex554 ) shows both constructions. The first two clauses are in a temporal relationship to the last clause, which is signalled by fthé `when'. This is not a subordinate relationship because fthé can also be used in independent clauses with the meaning of `that was when'. In the first clause, the single argument of the verb is bad `ground, earth'. This can be translated either as an reflexive / impersonal `the earth created (itself)' or as a passive `the earth was created'. In the second clause, matters are clear because the verb is in a transitive template which shows actor agreement with `father'  and undergoer agreement with `earth', thus: `the father created the earth'. The last clause is a resultative construction. The nominalised verb rifthzsi `hiding' takes the instrumental case (`with hiding'), which is best translated as a passive (`was hidden').

exe
bad fthé ŋafiyokwa... ŋafyf fthé bad wäfiyokwa... kidn ane rifthzsime zfrärm.\\
bad fthé ŋa fiyokwa (.) ŋafe=f fthé bad wä fiyokwa (.) kidn ane rifthz-si=me zf rärm\\
earth when::: /make (.) father=. when earth: >.::: /make (.) eternal fire hide- =.::: /be\\
`When the earth was made... when God made the earth... that eternal fire was hidden.' tci20120909-06KAB #61-63

exe
summary: Passive-like meanings in this language are expressed either by a middle-template verb that indexes a patient role in the absolutive case, or by a resultative construction in which a nominalised verb takes instrumental case. Neither construction is a dedicated passive; both can be interpreted with passive-like semantics. The example illustrates that one clause can be translated as passive, another clearly as transitive, and the final resultative clause as “was hidden.”

text:
Formally, reflexive / reciprocal clauses are encoded by (i) the verb form in the middle template and (ii) the argument noun phrase in the absolutive case. Ditransitives show exceptional grammatical behaviour in that the argument may be in the absolutive or ergative case. There is no distinction between reflexives and reciprocals other than the fact that singulars do not allow a reciprocal reading. Below I will describe how reflexive /reciprocals differ from intransitive and impersonal clause on the one hand, and from suppressed-object constructions on the other. This topic is also addressed in the description of the middle template ( middletemplatesubsection ).

In example ( ex566 ) the speaker talks about a ritual which chases away evil spirits. This rather gruesome ritual involves young men shooting at each other with blunt arrows. In the last clause of the example the noun phrase kabe `man' is in the absolutive case and the verb employs the middle template and indexes one argument. The verb rusi `shoot' has rather clear transitive semantics. Consequently, it invites a reciprocal interpretation in the middle template.

exe
kabe kwaruthrmth frkkarä. \\
kabe kwa ruthrmth frk=karä\\
man::: /shoot blood= \\
`The people were shooting at each other (until) they were bleeding.' tci20150906-10ABB #414

exe

In most cases only secondary information disambiguates between intransitive, impersonal and reflexive / reciprocal interpretations. By secondary information, I mean (i) context, (ii) grammatical devices which are not used solely for reflexive / reciprocal constructions, (iii) statistical tendencies of individual verbs. I will address these in turn. First, context is probably the most important, and it is evident that an example like ( ex566 ) is usually preceded or followed by a description which disambiguates the state of affairs. Secondly, speakers may choose to repeat the absolutive noun phrase to make clear that the intended reading should be a reciprocal one. Consider example ( ex567 ), which concludes a headhunting story. The pronoun fi occurs twice. Additionally, the utterance was accompanied by appropriate gestures to clarify the intended reciprocal meaning. The pronoun fi is marked with the exclusive enclitic =nzo. The repetition and the exclusive enclitic are secondary strategies which are not solely used to mark reflexive / reciprocal meanings. Note that the exclusive enclitic =nzo shows cognates in other Yam languages. In Nen, there is a set of reflexive / reciprocal pronouns which all end in nzo, for example benzo. In Komnzo, the exclusive clitic expresses the meaning of `only' without reflexive / reciprocal semantics.

exe
ni woga tüfrmäre nrä... bänema nzenme thden ane fof kwakwirm... woga finzo finzo kwafnzrmth.\\
ni woga tüfr=märe n rä (.) bäne=ma nzenme thd=en ane fof kwa kwirm (.) woga fi=nzo fi=nzo kwa fnnzrmth\\
man plenty=::: /be (.): =. middle =::: /run (.) man. =. =::: /kill\\
`We are not many... because this was going on in our middle... The people, this (group) and that (group) were killing each other.' tci20111107-01MAK #157-158

exe

Although stems may alternate between different morphological templates there is a statistical tendency for a particular stem to occur in a particular template. For example, typically transitive meanings ( rusi `shoot', zan `hit, kill', marasi `see') occur most of the time in the ambifixing transitive template. If such stems occur in a middle template, it invites a reflexive / reciprocal reading rather than an impersonal or intransitive one. We will see in the following section that the middle template can also be used for the suppressed-object construction ( suppressedobjectclause ). However, in the suppressed-object construction the noun phrase indexed in the verb form is marked for ergative case and not absolutive. On the other hand, stems which occur in the middle template most of the time ( maikasi `wash', bringsi `return') should be analysed as reflexiva tanta, even though they may occur in the ambifixing transitive template (`wash someone', `bring back someone'). Hence, there is a statistical tendency for stems to occur in a particular template, which helps to disambiguate between an impersonal or reflexive / reciprocal reading.

Next, I want to set reflexive /reciprocals apart from what I call the suppressed-object construction ( suppressedobjectclause ). The state of affairs in reflexive /reciprocals is such that the actor and patient can be exchanged. In Komnzo, both are expressed by one noun phrase which occurs in the absolutive case. Herein lies the formal difference from the suppressed-object construction. If the noun phrase kabe `people' in example ( ex566 ) was in the ergative case for example kabe=yé (man=. ) the sentence would mean `they were shooting (at sth.)'. This is the suppressed-object construction, which I describe in the following section ( suppressedobjectclause ). Note that the verb form kwaruthrmth remains the same, only the case marking changes.

For ditransitive verbs, the case marking is less fixed, and the argument noun phrase can appear in the absolutive as well as ergative case, both with a reflexive / reciprocal meaning. In example ( ex568 ), the verb form ŋarinth indexes only the subject, while the prefix slot is filled with the middle marker. The subject argument appears in the ergative ( nafa ). A suppressed-object reading is not possible with ditransitive verbs. Note that the argument could also occur in the absolutive case ( fi ). This would create a clause with two absolutive noun phrases. Hence, the choice between ergative and abolutive seems to be dependent on the kinds of referents. In ( ex568 ), both noun phrases are animate, and the use of the ergative case avoids confusion between agent (`they') and theme (`sisters').

exe
emoth nafa ŋarinth fof. \\
emoth nafa ŋa rinth fof\\
girl.::: /give \\
`They give each other sisters.' tci20120805-01ABB #158

exe

At this stage, it is impossible to investigate this topic further, because (i) noun phrase s are frequently omitted and (ii) as I have argued in ambifixingtemp, except for a few verbs ( yarisi `give', trikasi `tell', fänzsi `show') all ditransitive verbs are derived.
summary: Reflexive/reciprocal clauses in Komnzo are formally marked by the middle verb template together with an absolutive argument noun phrase, though ditransitives are exceptional in allowing either absolutive or ergative case. Reflexive and reciprocal meanings are not formally distinct except that singular forms cannot have a reciprocal reading, and interpretation is often disambiguated by context, repetition, exclusive enclitics, or verb-specific template tendencies. The passage also distinguishes these clauses from suppressed-object constructions, where the verb may look the same but the indexed noun phrase is ergative rather than absolutive.

text:
Suppressed- object clauses employ the middle template of the verb. The argument indexed in the verb is treated like an actor by the case system, i.e. it is flagged with the ergative case. The object may be overtly expressed with a noun phrase, but it is suppressed from indexation in the verb form.

I describe in middletemplatesubsection how almost all transitive verbs can enter into the suppressed-object construction for semantic as well as pragmatic reasons. For example, most of the time, the referents of suppressed-objects rank low in the animacy hierarchy. In example ( ex569 ), the speaker searches for her shoes and complains that her friend has been wearing them. We only know about the object of rgsi `wear' from the previous context since it is not expressed as a noun phrase, nor is the object indexed in the verb form. The semantics of rgsi renders a reflexive reading (`she wears herself') nonsensical. Additionally, the fact that the subject is in the ergative case ( naf ) rules out the reflexive / reciprocal interpretation. This is important because the verb form is identical between reflexive /reciprocals and the suppressed-object construction.

exe
ebar zfthnzo! naf rar ŋargwrm? \\
ebar zfth=nzo naf ra=r ŋa rgwrm\\
head base=. what=::: /wear\\
`Thickhead! Why was she wearing (the flipflops)?' tci20130901-04RNA #173

exe

Objects can be suppressed for pragmatic reasons, often in addition to their low rank on the animacy hierarchy. That is because the suppression of the object has the pragmatic effect of focussing the subject. Example ( ex570 ) is taken from a text about food taboos. This topic came up while talking about a very old woman, whose old age was ascribed to her respecting all food taboos. In the example, the speaker shifts the topic from the old woman to those people who did not respect food taboos. This shift of topic is achieved by (i) a fronted relative clause and (ii) the suppressed-object construction. As in the previous example, we only know about the object of rirksi `respect, avoid' from the preceding context.

exe
fi mafa keke kwarirkwrmth... watik tekmär esufakwa. \\
fi mafa keke kwarirkwrmth... watik tekmär esufakwa\\
but who..::: /respect (.) then duration=::: /grow.old\\
`But those who did not respect (the food taboos)... well, they grew old quickly.' tci20120922-26DAK #26-27

exe

Although the object is suppressed from indexation in the verb form, it may occur as a noun phrase in the clause. In example ( ex571 ), the speaker talks about garden magic and people who steal the soil from other people's gardens. In the relative clause, the object bad `ground' is suppressed from indexation in the verb, yet it appears as a noun phrase. The subject is indexed in the verb suffix and the corresponding noun phrase, the relative pronoun mafa, is in the ergative case.

exe
nä kabenzo nnzä wawa gamokarä erä bad mafa ŋakarkwrth. \\
nä kabe=nzo nnzä wawa gamo=karä e rä bad mafa ŋa karkwrth\\
man= perhaps yam spell=::: /be ground who..::: /take\\
`Perhaps only other people, who take the soil away, have yam magic.'\\ tci20130822-08JAA #42

exe

The suppressed-object may also be a relative clause, as in example ( ex572 ), which is taken from a picture stimulus task.

exe
emothf ŋatrikwr monme zffnzr. \\
emoth=f ŋa trikwr mon=me zf fnnzr\\
girl=.::: /tell how=: >.::: /hit\\
`The girl tells (the story of) how he hit her.' tci20120925MAE #102

exe

There are a few verbs which always occur in the suppressed-object construction. A few examples are: yonasi `drink', fathasi `marry', frzsi `fish/net (poison-root)', naf- `talk, speak' and karksi `pull'. The stem karksi can occur in a transitive template with the meaning `take'. If it occurs in a suppressed-object construction, it means `pull'. I analyse these as two different lexical items, because there is a difference in the semantics as well as the combinatorics of the stem. With other verbs there is only a statistical tendency to enter this construction. For example, yarizsi `hear' occurs 104 times in the corpus; 25 times the object is indexed and 79 times it is suppressed. In other words, in only about a quarter of all tokens of yarizsi does the verb mean `hear X'. In the other three quarters of tokens of yarizsi, it means `hear (sth.)'. In ( ex573 ), we see an example of yarizsi and rfnaksi `taste' in the suppressed-object construction. The speaker explains how the news of the beginning yam harvest spread from East to West, from village to village.

exe
watik, we masu karé kwekaristh ``oh, nafa z zärfnth!'' \\
watik, we masu karé kwe karisth oh nafa z zä rfnth\\
then also masu village=.:: /hear oh.::: /taste\\
`Then the Masu people always heard (the other village): ``Oh, they have already tasted (the yams)!''' tci20131013-01ABB #363

exe
summary:
Suppressed-object clauses use the verb’s middle template, and the indexed argument is treated as an actor by the case system, so it takes ergative case while the object is not indexed in the verb. The object may be omitted for semantic or pragmatic reasons, often because it is low in animacy or because suppressing it shifts focus to the subject, though it can still appear as a noun phrase or even as a relative clause.

The passage also notes that some verbs are especially associated with this construction: a few always occur in it, while others show a statistical tendency to do so. In some cases, suppression changes interpretation or is needed to distinguish the construction from reflexive/reciprocal readings.

text:
This section deals with prototypical transitive clauses, which are transitive in their verb morphology, i.e. they are built from the ambifixing transitive template, as well as their noun phrase syntax, i.e. the actor argument is flagged with the ergative and the undergoer argument is in the absolutive. Therefore, suppressed-object constructions ( suppressedobjectclause ) can be described as non-prototypical transitive clauses because (i) the verb appears in the middle template, and (ii) the object noun phrase is frequently omitted. However, noun phrases can generally be dropped in all clause types. The ambifixing verb template is described in ambifixingtemp. An example of a transitive clause is given in ( ex574 ).

exe
nzürna ŋaref bäne ŋad yrtmakwa. \\
nzürna ŋare=f bäne ŋad y rtmakwa\\
spirit woman=.: string: >.::: /cut\\
`The nzürna woman cut that string.' tci20120827-03KUT #142

exe
summary: Prototypical transitive clauses are defined by both verb morphology and noun phrase syntax: they use the ambifixing transitive template, with the actor marked ergative and the undergoer in absolutive. Suppressed-object constructions are treated as non-prototypical transitives because the verb is in the middle template and the object noun phrase is often omitted, though noun phrases can generally be dropped in all clause types.

text:
Ditransitive clauses employ the same template as transitive clauses. However, the valency changing prefix a- shifts the reference of the verb prefix from the direct object to the indirect object. The corresponding noun phrase appears in dative case. This is described in ambifixingtemp. Note that the a- prefix may increase as well as decrease the valency of a verb, hence, the label `` valency changing prefix'' ( morphologicaltemplates ).

Example ( ex575 ) shows the verbs trikasi `tell' and fänzsi `show'. The recipient arguments are flagged for dative case and the respective arguments are indexed in the two verbs.

exe
nzone ŋafyn bäin ane trikasi yatrikwath... nzunwä ŋafyf bäif zwafäsa.\\
nzone ŋafe=n bäi=n ane trika-si ya trikwath (.) nzun=wä ŋafe=f bäi=f zwa fäsa\\. father=. bäi=. tell-: >.::: /tell (.). = father=. bäi=.: >::: /show\\
`They told that story to my father Bäi... and father Bäi showed (it) to me.'\\ tci20110802ABB #18-20

exe

Ditransitive clauses may also contain cognate objects, as in ( ex575 ) trikasi yatrikwath `they told him the story'. Another example is yathugsi `trick (v)', which often occurs with gaso `trick, lie'.

In ambifixingtemp, I argued that ditransitive should be recognised as a category even though most ditransitive verbs are derived from transitives by (i) adding the valency change prefix a-, which (ii) changes the reference of the verb prefix to an indirect object ( goal, recipient, beneficiary ) and (iii) putting the respective argument noun phrase in dative case. The same strategy can be used to raise possessors in the cross-referencing of the verb. In example ( ex576 ) it is the possessor ( nzone `my' ), which is indexed in the verb, and not the possessed ( miyo `desire/wish'. ).

exe
nzone miyo kwa wabthakwr.\\
nzone miyo kwa wo-a-bthak-w-r- \\. desire. - -finish. - - \\: >::: /finish\\
`You will fulfil my wish.' tci20130823-06CAM #23

exe

The ditransitive pattern is very productive and almost all transitive verbs can enter this construction. Most verbs retain their transitive semantics, but can index a beneficiary of the event. For example, in ( ex577 ), the verb fsisi `count' in the clause takes the object `yam suckers'. The ditransitive pattern only adds a beneficiary which is indexed in the verb.

exe
nä efothen... wawa tafo yafsinzake... babuan.\\
nä efoth=en (.) wawa tafo yafsinzake (.) babua=n\\
day= (.) yam sucker: >.::: /count (.) babua=. \\
`Some day... we counted yam suckers for him... for Babua.'\\ tci20120814ABB #165-167

exe

As I pointed out in prefixingverbsec, prefixing verbs (intransitives) can enter the same pattern, in which a beneficiary or raised possessor, in dative and possessive case respectively, is indexed in the verb form. Example ( ex741 ) is taken from a recording where two speakers discuss the content of a picture card. The prefixing verb -thn `be lying' in the example does not index the objects that are lying on the ground, but the possessor instead.

exe
ra kwa nm bäne wäthn?... nafane nainai?\\
ra kwa nm bäne wä thn (.) nafane nainai\\
what maybe:.::: /be.lying (.). sweet.potato\\
`What (of hers) might be lying there?... her sweet potatoes?' tci20111004RMA #108

exe
summary: Ditransitive clauses use the same basic template as transitive clauses, but the valency-changing prefix a- shifts verb indexing from the direct object to an indirect object, which is marked in the dative case. This pattern is highly productive: most transitive verbs can be used ditransitively to index a recipient, beneficiary, or raised possessor, while some prefixing intransitive verbs can also participate in the same construction.

text:
Experiencer-object constructions express bodily, mental and emotional processes (`get sunburned', `shiver in fear', `be angry'). These are framed as transitive clauses in which the stimulus acts on the experiencer. Constructions of this type have been examined by Pawley et al. for Kalam ( Pawley:2000vp) showing that experiencer-objects as well as experiencer-subjects are found in the semantic domain of bodily and mental processes. Note that the notion of experiencer is slightly extended here to include bodily processes in addition to mental or emotional ones. Komnzo confirms their findings. In terms of their morpho-syntax, experiencer-object constructions are characterised by the following criteria: (i) the stimulus argument appears in the ergative, (ii) the stimulus is indexed by a default in the verb suffix, (iii) the experiencer occurs in the absolutive case, and (iv) the word order is UAV ( undergoer actor verb).

Consider the two ways of expressing a feeling of hunger in the elicited examples in ( ex5788 ). In ( ex578 ) the experiencer is the subject of the copula clause, but in ( ex579 ) it is the object of the verb rmatksi `cut'. In the latter the feeling of hunger is portrayed as somewhat stronger. Note that the choice of verb is not entirely fixed. One can replace rmatksi `cut' with a light verb, for example rä- `do' (`hunger does me'), or with the phasal verb bthaksi `finish' (`hunger finishes me'), thereby changing the degree or intensity of the experienced feeling. Thus, the experiencer-object construction is one possible way to express mental and bodily processes.

exe

xlist
nzä frasi worä \\
nzä frasi wo rä\\. hunger::: /be\\
`I am hungry.'

nzä frasif wortmakwr \\
nzä frasi=f wo rtmakwr\\. hunger=.: >::: /cut\\
`I am hungry. / I am starving.' (Lit: `Hunger cuts me.')

xlist
exe

Examples like ( ex578 ) were given to me in elicitation, when asking `How do I say `I am hungry?'. I first encountered experiencer-object constructions in more natural situations, for example in overhearing conversations or when translating recordings. Komnzo speakers explicitly regard experiencer-object constructions as more original and creative language. Therefore, it seems natural that these were rarely offered in the context of elicitation. Experiencer-object constructions portray a situation in much more colourful terms. They often evoke some kind of emotional reaction (laughter or sympathy) from the audience, as in ( ex685 ), where a woman describes what happened to her as a small child when she was hiding in a tree from a pig.

exe
nzä wthf warfo bä kwräbth.\\
nzä wth=f warfo bä kwrä bth\\. faeces= above: >::: /finish\\
`I really had to take a dump there on top (of the tree).' (Lit: `Excretions finish me.') tci20150919-05LNA #117

exe

Experiencer-object constructions express bodily and mental processes, and it is this internal stimulus which `acts' on the experiencer. Two text examples were given in the description of the ergative case ( ergcase ) and are repeated here as ( ex580 ) and ( ex581 ).

exe
nokuyé fthé sabtha.\\
noku=yé fthé sa btha\\
anger=. when: >.:: /finish\\
`That is when he got really angry.' (lit. `Anger finished him.')\\ tci20120909-06KAB #39

exe

exe
wtrif z zwefaf.\\
wtri=f z zwe faf\\
fear=: >::: /hold\\
`I am already scared.' (lit. `Fear holds me.') tci20130901-04RNA #164

exe

The stimulus noun phrase can be modified, for example with a nominal compound. In example ( ex582 ) the stimulus miyo `desire' is modified by two elements yielding kabe zan miyo `desire to kill people'. This example is repeated from the discussion of complex heads in compounds-subsec.

exe
baf fthé sräbth nima... kabe zan miyof.\\
baf fthé srä bth nima (.) kabe zan miyo=f\\.. when: >.::: /finish like.this (.) man hitting desire= \\
`That is when this overcomes him... the bloodlust for people.' (lit. `People killing desire finishes him.') tci20130903-04RNA #84-85

exe

Experiencer-object constructions differ in their basic word order from other clauses in that the experiencer, the object, comes first. This can be explained by the special semantics of the experiencer-object construction, in which the most salient element is the experiencer. However, most of the examples in this section do not include an overt noun phrase. One example from the corpus is given in ( ex583 ). Note that the speaker corrects himself in this example. He first uses the absolutive ( frfr ) `shiver', but then repeats the same noun in the ergative ( frfré ).

exe
nge fäth frfr a frfré n safum.\\
nge fäth frfr a frfr=é n sa fum\\
child shiver ah shiver=.: >.::: /pull\\
`The small child was almost shivering' (lit. `The shivers were about to pull him.') tci20130901-04YUK #26

exe

Note that in ( ex583 ) and ( ex580 ), the noun phrase is marked with the non-singular ergative ( =é ), while the verb indexes a singular actor. All other examples in the corpus employ the singular ergative ( =f ). In fact, these are the only examples in the corpus, where an inanimate referent receives a non-singular ergative. Note that there is no number distinction for inanimate referent for all case enclitics. We can draw two conlcusions from this observation. First, experiencer object construction give the stimulus are somewhat elevated status of animacy, i.e. the stimulus is portrayed as being animate. Secondly, the fact that the verb inflection is singular, rather than plural, is evidence for the limited grammatical behaviour of property nouns. Property nouns do not trigger agreement in the verb and the only construction in which property nouns show quasi-agreement is the experiencer-object construction. I call this ``quasi-agreement'' because it is default in the suffix ( propertynouns-sec ).

The second domain of experiencer-object constructions is that of bodily processes, as in ( ex583 ). A few more examples of this type are given in ( ex584 - ex587 ).

exe
zä zf fthé thkarf yafiyokwa ziyé.\\
zä zf fthé thkar=f ya fiyokwa z= yé\\
when hardness=: >.::: /make =.:: /be\\
`That is when it got stuck right here.' (lit. `Hardness made it.')\\ tci20120922-09DAK #18
summary:
Experiencer-object constructions in Komnzo express bodily, mental, and emotional processes by framing them as transitive clauses in which the stimulus acts on the experiencer. Morphosyntactically, the stimulus is ergative and indexed by a default verb suffix, while the experiencer is absolutive and typically comes first in UAV word order; the passage also notes that these constructions can make the feeling seem stronger or more vivid than experiencer-subject alternatives.

The text further argues that such constructions are perceived by speakers as more original and creative, which may explain why they were less often elicited than encountered in natural discourse. In some examples, the stimulus is treated as somewhat animate and the verb shows only limited “quasi-agreement,” especially with property nouns.

text:
exe
exe
nzä sukufa zürnf wortmakwr.\\
nzä sukufa zürn=f wo rtmakwr kwan=en\\. tobacco smoke=: >::: /cut throat= \\
`The tobacco is very strong.' (lit. `Tobacco smoke cuts me.') 1pt [overheard]

exe
exe
nzrmf wortmakwr kwanen.\\
nzrm=f wo rtmakwr kwan=en\\
bitterness=: >::: /cut throat= \\
`It is very sour.' (lit. `Bitterness cuts me.') 1pt [overheard]

exe
exe
watik nzfrä... efothf nfariwr.\\
watik nzf rä (.) efoth=f n fariwr\\
enough::: /be (.) sun=: >::: /dry\\
`We have done enough... We are burning in the sun.' (lit. `The sun dries us.') tci20111119-03ABB #200

exe
summary: The passage gives examples of figurative expressions in which an experience is described as affecting the body, such as “tobacco smoke cuts me” for strong tobacco, “bitterness cuts me” for sourness, and “the sun dries us” for intense heat. These examples show that physical sensations or qualities are expressed through verbs of bodily harm or dryness.

text:
Cognate objects are a common phenomenon in Komnzo. Examples ( ex731 - ex730 ) contain a nominalised verb and an inflected verb. In all three examples, the nominalisation and the inflected verb form are of the same lexeme. Hence, ( ex731 ) translates literally as `I tell them the telling'. The inflected verb indexes the indirect object  and as with other ditransitive verbs, trikasi is the direct object of the verb.

exe
nze ane trik asi ä trik wé.\\
nze ane trik-si ä trikwé\\. tell-: >::: /tell\\
`I tell them the story.' (lit. `I tell them the telling.') tci20111119-03ABB #161

exe

There is an analytical problem with verbs which occur in the middle template. Example ( ex730 ) translates literally as `He laughs the laughter' or as `He laughter-laughs'. The middle template used in ( ex729 ) and ( ex730 ) only indexes the subject argument, not the object. Because of this, it cannot be determined whether the nominalisations maikasi `washing' and borsi `laughing' function as objects or whether they function predicatively. We will see below that a predicative function is a possible analysis in some cases. From this perspective, cognate object s and predicative nominal s in light verb constructions can be portrayed as contiguous phenomena. Light verb constructions are described in the following section ( lightverb ).

exe
maik asi bä ŋa mayuk wro.\\
maik-si bä ŋa maikwro\\
wash-:::: /wash\\
`I will wash there.' (lit. `I washing-wash.') tci20130823-06STK #53

exe
exe
bor si ŋa bor wr.\\
borsi ŋa borwr\\
laugh-::: /laugh\\
`He laughs.' (lit. `He laughs the laughing.') tci20111004TSA #128

exe

A second problem is that many verbs lack regular nominalisations, which are formed with the suffix -si. These verbs use a common noun, as in example ( ex564 ). The adjective kwosi `dead' functions adverbially and adds the meaning of a deep sleep. The noun etfth `sleep', however, is semantically fully included in the meaning of the verb rug- `sleep', just as the regular nominalisation borsi `laugh' is included in the stem of the inflected verb in ( ex730 ). As a consequence, etfth is optional and the sentence would be grammatical without it. Note that the same is true of examples ( ex731 - ex730 ).

exe
fi etfth kwosi sfrugrm.\\
fi etfth kwosi sf rugrm\\. sleep dead.::: /sleep\\
`He was sleeping soundly.' (lit. `He was dead sleep sleeping.')\\ tci20120904-02MAB #98

exe

For want of a better term, I label examples like ( ex564 ) ` pseudo-cognate object ' constructions. They are unlike cognate objects because the verb stem and the nominal element are formally not related. Other examples are rnzür- `dance, sing' and wath `dance (n), song' and -nor `shout, emit sound' and kwan `shout (n)'. Although the verb stem and the noun are not cognate, distributional evidence shows that they stand in the same relationship as an inflected verb and the corresponding regular nominalisation with -si. For example, the phasal verb bthaksi `finish' takes the noun wath `dance (n), song' to mean `finish singing'. This is because there is no regular nominalisation available for the verb rnzür- `dance, sing'.

The noun in these constructions is not always redundant. For example, it can be modified as the head of a compound, thereby modifying the predicate. In ( ex565 ), the noun etfth `sleep' occurs in a compound modified by efoth `day' indicating that the speaker was sleeping during the day.

exe
efoth etfth kwofrugrm e zizi.\\
efoth etfth kwof rugrm e zizi\\
day sleep::: /sleep until afternoon\\
`I was sleeping during the day until the afternoon.' (lit. `I was day-sleep sleeping.')\\ tci20111119-03ABB #31

exe

This kind of predicate modification is developed to varying degrees. The best example is the intransitive verb nor- `shout, emit a sound', which again lacks an infinitive and instead kwan `shout (n), call' is used. Hence, kwan yanor `He shouts the shout' or `He emits the shout' is a common expression. The relatively large set of ideophones ( ideophones-sec ) enter into compounds of the type ideophone + kwan, as in sö kwan `sound of wallabies grunting' or nzam kwan `the sound of smacking one's lips'. Most auditory sensations are expressed in this construction with the verb nor-. In example ( ex732 ), the gurgling sound of a headhunter's victim is described.

Instead of kwan, one can use the noun frk `blood' with the verb nor- `shout' to express that someone is bleeding, as in example ( ex734 ), which comes from the description of a picture card.

The second example is the noun wanzo `dream' which can be used with rug- `sleep' (instead of etfth `sleep (n)'). In example ( ex735 ), the speaker talks about the mythological significance of the bird of paradise, when it appears in one's dream.

summary: Komnzo has common cognate object constructions in which a nominalised verb and an inflected verb are forms of the same lexeme, though the inflected verb indexes only the subject or indirect object, making the nominal element potentially object-like or predicative. The language also has “pseudo-cognate object” constructions where the verb lacks a regular nominalisation and instead combines with an unrelated noun that functions similarly, sometimes redundantly but sometimes as a meaningful modifier in compounds or idiomatic predicate expressions.

text:
There are a handful of ( intransitive ) verbs for which pseudo-cognate constructions are possible, even though there is a regular nominalisation with -si available. For example, bznsi `work (v.i.)' can occur together with znsä `work (n)'. Another example is mthizsi `suffer', which can occur with zi `pain', as in example ( ex736 ).

exe
zi swathizrm... ekri zi... kofä ysma. \\
zi swa thizrm (.) ekri zi (.) kofä ys=ma\\
pain.::: /suffer (.) flesh pain (.) fish thorn= \\
`He was in pain... body pain... from the fish spike.' tci20100905ABB #91-93

exe

We have seen above that cognate and pseudo-cognate constructions are similar to light verb constructions in that a nominal element contributes to the meaning of the predicate. They are markedly different in the degree of modification, because light verbs are much more general in their semantics ( rä- `do', fiyoksi `make', ko- `become'). It might be best to view this as a cline: at one end of the spectrum we have cognate object constructions, where the nominalisation of the verb occurs together with the same verb, as in examples ( ex731 - ex730 ). On the other end of the spectrum we have light verb constructions, where the nominal element not only carries most of the meaning of the predicate, but it always differs formally from the verb. Light verbs are described in the next section.
summary: Some intransitive verbs can appear in pseudo-cognate constructions even when a regular nominalization in -si exists, as in bznsi ‘work’ with znsä ‘work (n)’ and mthizsi ‘suffer’ with zi ‘pain.’ These constructions are similar to light verb constructions because a nominal element contributes to the predicate’s meaning, but they differ in how much modification is involved: light verbs are semantically more general. The passage suggests a cline from cognate object constructions, where the verb and its nominalization are formally the same, to light verb constructions, where the nominal carries most of the meaning and is formally distinct from the verb.

text:
There are number of light verbs in Komnzo. These are rä- `do', ko- `become', fiyoksi `make' and the two phasal verbs thkäfsi `start' and bthaksi `finish'. The first two are interesting from a lexical perspective. The light verb rä- is build from the same stem as the copula. In a prefixing template this stem means `be', but in an ambifixing template it means `do'. The second stem ko- only occurs in ambifixing templates, where it can mean `speak' or `become'. Although these are only statistical tendencies, in the middle template ko- usually means `become', whereas in a transitive template it usually means `speak'.

The light verb `do' is usually used in the middle template indexing only the subject argument. A very frequent collocation is with fam `thought', thus, literally: `do thoughts' means `think'. Examples ( ex590 ) and ( ex591 ) are taken from a picture stimulus task. Note that fam is not indexed in the verb form, even if the light verb indexes an object. In ( ex591 ), fam functions predicatively, and a literal translation of `He thinks of her' is `He thought-does her'.

exe
wati, ane fof yamnzr fam ŋarär.\\
wati ane fof ya mnzr fam ŋa rär\\
then.::: /sit thought::: /do\\
`Okay, this one is sitting. He is thinking.' tci20111004RMA #133

exe
exe
zane emoth fam wrär anema yatrikwr nafan.\\
zane emoth fam w rär ane=ma ya trikwr nafan\\: girl thought: >.::: /do =: >.::: /tell. \\
`He thinks of that girl and he tells him about her.' tci20111004RMA #52

exe

This is a general feature of light verbs. They require a nominal element which functions predicatively. Hence, we find predicative nominal s in both intransitive ( ex590 ) and transitive structures ( ex591 ). In these examples, the predicative nominal was the noun fam, but very often property nouns are used for this function, especially property nouns with more event-oriented semantics. In example ( ex592 ), the speaker remarks that his dogs have disappeared. The meaning of disappearing is expressed by the property noun ofe `absent/absence'.

exe
fi kafar mane erera näbi ane ofe ŋarerath.\\
fi kafar mane e rära näbi ane ofe ŋa rärath.\\
but big which::: /be one absent::: /do\\
`But the big (dogs), they disappeared for good.' tci20111119-03ABB #70

exe

The light verb ko- `become' shows similar behaviour. It can appear with nominal s as in ( ex593 ) with the adjective kafar `big'. But often `become' occurs with property nouns which function predicatively. In ( ex594 ), the property noun wefwef `excited/excitement' contributes most of the meaning of the event.

exe

`Well, today she has become already old without (having) children.'\\ tci20120814ABB #214-215

The light verb `become' together with the property noun miyatha `knowledge' is used to express coming into the state of knowing something, literally `become knowledge(able)'. In example ( ex595 ) a man, who fell off a coconut palm in an attempt to steal palm wine, is badly insulted. The imperative miyatha käkor can be translated as both `you know it!' or `you feel it!'.

exe
fof nrä! miyatha käkor! buŋame zakiyar!\\

Example ( ex596 ) is about the tütü bird (Pheasant Coucal), who used to be the custodian of fire before people knew about it. In the example, they find out about the bird's secret. Note that the light verb `become' indexes the tütü bird (. ). Thus, the predicative nominal miyatha `knowledgeable' in the light verb construction can be used with an intransitive ( ex595 ) or transitive sense ( ex596 ).

exe
nä kayé... miyatha wkonzath. ``oh budben mni rä fof.''\\
nä kayé (.) miyatha w konzath oh budben mni rä fof\\

`One day... they found out about her. ``Oh, so the fire is really with you.'''\\ tci20131008KAB #10-11

The verb fiyoksi `make' can occur as a prototypical transitive verb without the ``semantic assistance'' of a predicative nominal. However, it commonly occurs as a light verb. In example ( ex597 ), we find two occurences of fiyoksi. The first token indexes zrin `problem, burden' (. ) as its object argument, and fiyoksi can be translated as `create'. The second token of fiyoksi indexes the subject. In the latter, the predicative nominal durua `help' contributes most of the semantic content of the predicate.

exe
nzä nima ``bone zrin rä bone nagayf ane zrin zwafiyokwr keke kwa monme durua ŋafiyokwre "\\

`I said: ``This is your problem. Your child has created this problem. We will not help.''' tci20120922-24STK #22

Analogous to the other light verbs, fiyoksi can be used in a transitive structure. In example ( ex598 ), an infamous sorcerer is annoyed by a few other men. The main semantic contribution to the event comes from the property noun thythy `nuisance', while the object indexed in the light verb is the sorcerer (. ).

summary: Komnzo has several light verbs: rä- ‘do’, ko- ‘become’, fiyoksi ‘make’, and the phasal verbs thkäfsi ‘start’ and bthaksi ‘finish’. Rä-, ko-, and fiyoksi commonly combine with a predicative nominal or property noun that carries most of the meaning, such as fam ‘thought’ in ‘think’, ofe ‘absent’ in ‘disappear’, and miyatha ‘knowledgeable’ in ‘find out’. These light verbs can appear in both intransitive and transitive structures, with the light verb indexing different arguments while the nominal element supplies the main semantic content.

text:
The two phasal verbs usually take nominalised verbs as their complements ( phasalcomplements ), but they can also be supplemented by property nouns with more event-oriented semantics. Hence, they exhibit the same double life as full verbs and light verbs as fiyoksi. Two examples of thkäfsi `start' functioning as a light verb are given below. In ( ex599 ), a man is trying to enter the house in which two children are hiding. The phasal verb indexes the two children, while the semantic content of the event comes solely from the property noun zirkn `persistence'.

exe
wati zänfrefa yanyak nagayé kma n zirkn thrathkäf... zirkn.\\
wati zän frefa yan yak nagayé kma n zirkn thra thkäf (.) zirkn\\
then::: /come.up.:::: /walk children persistence: >::: /start (.) persistence\\
`Then, he came up from the river, he walked. He was about to start hassling the two children... hassling (them).' tci20100905ABB #111

exe

In example ( ex600 ), a malevolent spirit is trying to persuade a man to stay the night in her house. Again, the property noun garamgaram `sweet-talk' expresses most of the semantics of the event.

exe
garamgaram srethkäf.\\
garamgaram sre thkäf\\
sweet.talk: >.::: /start\\
`She started sweet-talking him.' tci20120901-01MAK #88

exe

As I have shown above, light verbs ( rä- `do', ko- `become', fiyoksi `make', thkäfsi `start' and bthaksi `finish') require semantic assistance from nominal predicates. However, nominal predicates can be found with other verbs, i.e. full verbs. In the following examples, the concepts of `being concentrated' ( ex601 ) and `being locked in' ( ex602 ) are expressed by the property nouns mogu `concentration' and ttw `inertia', respectively. Both meanings could be expressed with light verbs, for example ( ex601 ) could be expressed as mogu ŋaräré `I am concentrating' (lit. `I am concentration-doing'). The two examples employ full verbs instead, which should be understood as a more idiosyncratic way of speaking.

exe
biskar mnifnzo mogu kwofkämgwrm \\
biskar mni=f=nzo mogu kwof kämgwrm\\

`Cooking the cassava took all my attention. (lit. `Cassava cooking concentration blocked me.')' tci20111119-03ABB #79

exe
exe

ttw zwe rmänth wati fobo thu fnnzrmth\\

`They always closed off (the village). Then, they were killing them.'\\ tci20120818ABB #46-47

exe

I point out in verbs-sec that verbs are considered to be a closed word class in Komnzo. Part of the argumentation is based on the observation that loanwords, which are verbs in the donor language, commonly end up as property nouns in a light verb construction. One such example was shown in ( ex597 ) with the property noun durua `help', which is a transitive verb in Motu. Below, two examples with English loans are given. In ( ex603 ), the verb fiyoksi indexes the object zokwasi `words', while the loanword senis `change' expresses most of the semantics (lit. `I will not change-make the words'). In ( ex604 ), the middle verb rä- `do' is supplemented by the English loan zek `check' (lit. `I check-do for water').

exe

zokwasi keke kwa senis thrä fiyothé\\

`I went down to the creek in Mäbri to check for water, but no (water).'\\ tci20130903-03MKW #146-147

exe

For situations of language contact, Heine and Kuteva describe how minor patterns in a language can become major patterns ( Heine:2005wp). It is clear that light verb constructions are not a minor pattern in Komnzo. However, it seems evident that with more ( verb ) loans entering the language, light verb constructions will become even more widely used.
summary: The passage explains that Komnzo phasal verbs usually combine with nominalized verbs, but they can also take property nouns with event-like meanings, creating light-verb constructions in which the phasal verb carries little of the event semantics. It also shows that Komnzo verbs can appear as full verbs with nominal predicates in more idiosyncratic expressions, and that loan verbs from other languages are often adapted into property nouns used in light-verb constructions, supporting the claim that verbs form a closed class in Komnzo.

text:
Content questions in Komnzo are formed by replacing the respective noun phrase with an interrogative. Word order may or may not be changed for pragmatic purposes. As content questions are always pragmatically motivated, the element which is asked about is automatically focussed. Therefore, the interrogative is often found in fronted position, but fronting is not part of question formation. Example ( ex701 ) shows an example with the interrogative ra `what'.

exe
nafafis zräs ``be ranzo kayé thwanfiyokwr?'' \\
nafa-fis zrä s be ra=nzo kayé thwan fiyokwr\\. -husband: >.::: /ask. what= yesterday: >:::: /make\\
`Her husband asked her: ``Just what have you done to them yesterday?'''\\ tci20120901-01MAK #163

exe

Example ( ex713 ) shows an example where the interrogative occurs inside a complex noun phrase `whose sister'. Note that the noun phrase which contains the interrogative has been fronted for pragmatic reasons. This is an example of a rhetorical question, because it came up in a discussion about the type of punitive actions one would launch against one's brothers-in-law.

exe
``mafane emoth be zufnzrm?'' nima fof skonzé \\
maf=ane emoth be zu fnnzrm nima fof s konzé\\

```Whose sister were you beating?'' that is what you must say to him.'\\ tci20120805-01ABB #219

Polar questions are often structurally identical to indicative statements but they have a rising intonation contour, as in ( ex702 ) and ( ex703 ). Additionally the iamitive particle z `already' can be used even though the verb is in the non-past ( ex702 ).

Question tags like o keke `or not' can be added, which also receive a rising intonation.

summary:
In Komnzo, content questions are formed by replacing the relevant noun phrase with an interrogative, and word order may be adjusted only for pragmatic reasons such as focus; fronting of the interrogative is common but not required by the grammar of question formation. Polar questions are usually structurally identical to declarative statements, distinguished mainly by rising intonation, though the iamitive particle *z* ‘already’ may appear even with non-past verbs.

Alternative questions are formed by disjunctive coordination with *o* ‘or’, either between clauses or between noun phrases. Question tags such as *o keke* ‘or not’ can also be added, and they too are pronounced with rising intonation.

At the clause level, negation is expressed periphrastically with the negator keke in preverbal position, as in example ( ex748 ). See tam-particles-subsec for more information on keke and its variant kyo.

One exception is the prohibitive construction ( apprehensivem ). This construction consists of the potential particle kma, the apprehensive clitic m=, and the verb in the imperative. The apprehensive clitic may attach either to the verb or to the potential particle. This construction is best translated into English as `must not' as can be seen in example ( ex749 ). Note that the negator cannot be included in this construction.

nznäbrimath ``bä kmam thiyaké! kafarnzo ni nyak!''. \\

Negation at the level of the constituent can be expressed in a number of ways. The word matak `nothing' is used to express non-existence, usually in a copula clause. This is shown in example ( ex750 ) where a man takes notice that he is alone in the village. Matak can also be used in a non-verb predication, for example nge matak `(there were) no children'. Alternatively, any noun phrase can be negated by using the privative case marker =mär. This is described in privcase.

Negative indefinites expressing `none whatsoever' or `nothing at all' are constructed by adding the negator keke to a noun phrase that includes the indefinite marker nä. For example, nä kabe means `some man' or `someone', but kabe nä keke means `nobody at all'. Note that the indefinite is always postposed in this construction. The same can be achieved by adding nä to an interrogative, as in ( ex765 ). I describe this topic in more detail in indefinite-sec.

summary:
At the clause level, negation is normally expressed periphrastically with the preverbal negator **keke**. An exception is the prohibitive construction, which uses the potential particle **kma**, the apprehensive clitic **m=**, and an imperative verb, meaning roughly “must not,” and it cannot include the negator.  

At the constituent level, **matak** expresses non-existence, especially in copular or non-verbal predications, and any noun phrase can also be negated with the privative case marker **=mär**. Negative indefinites such as “nobody at all” or “nothing at all” are formed by combining **keke** with a noun phrase containing the indefinite marker **nä**, with the indefinite element appearing after the noun phrase.

text:
This section describes the combination of two or more predicates. There are three parameters involving the coding of complex clauses. The first parameter is the verb inflection. Are both predicates fully inflected or is one of them nominalised? The second parameter is the way, how an interclausal relationship between two fully inflected predicates is marked. This often involves demonstratives marked for case. The third parameter are syntactic restrictions in one of the two clauses. These parameters allow us to decide whether a particular clause combination should be analysed as coordination or subordination. Note that the first parameter supersedes the other two, in that nominalised predicates are always analysed as subordinate clauses, and the other two parameters do not apply. Only if two clauses contain inflected verbs, these two parameters help to identify the relationship between them. For example, relative clauses are structurally similar to content questions, but they differ in two points. First, they are usually headed by the relativised element, which is in some sense the answer to the question posed by the relative clause. Secondly, relative clauses have a more rigid structure than questions. Hence, they are analysed as a type of subordination. On the other hand, complements of knowledge consist of one clause with a predicative nominal ( miyatha `knowledge') and the copula. The epistemic content can be expressed by a separate clause, which shows no syntactic dependency to the first. It follows that in some cases these parameters fail and only semantic criteria can be applied.

I want to give a few examples, to show that there is a cline of syntactic integration between two clauses. Givón provides a functional explanation to the various degrees of syntactic integration: ``the stronger the semantic bond between two events, the more extensive will be the syntactic integration of the two clauses into a single though complex clause'' ( Givon:2001syntax). As we will see, Komnzo supports this observation to some extent. I choose the domain of `cause' to illustrate this below. The clearest way to mark a causer is by putting the element in the ergative case. In Komnzo nominalised verbs can be used in this way ( ex662 ). In the example, a Marind headhunter tries to distract his victims by imitating the sound that dogs make when chewing bones, but he ends up only distracting himself. The phrase ane wäsifnzo `only that cracking' functions as a clausal subject. The event `crack' and the event `close' are tightly integrated. They occur simultaneously and they stand in direct causal relation.

exe
bäne thuwänzrm fof... zarfa surmänwrm ane wäsifnzo.\\
bäne thu wänzrm fof (.) zarfa su rmänwrm ane wä-si=f=nzo\\:: >::: /crack fof (.) ear: >.::: /close crack- = = \\
`He was cracking those (coconut shells)... This cracking was blocking his ears.'\\ tci20120818ABB #67-68

exe

The characteristic case is used for adverbial adjuncts marking origin and cause. In example ( ex663 ), mni frazsi functions as an adverbial clause. The predicate `be weak' and the event `extinguish' occurred at different times, but they stand in a causal relation.

exe
komnzo tayo zwrä mni frazsima.\\
komnzo tayo z=wo rä mni fraz-si=ma\\
only weak =::: /be fire extinguish- = \\
`I am just weak here from extinguishing the fire.' tci20120922-24STL #21

exe

Komnzo has a recognitional demonstrative pronoun, which can function in a number of ways ( recognitional-pronoun-subsec ). It is frequently used in `tip-of-the-tongue' situations. Example ( ex664 ) explains why a particular woman in Rouku grew very old, while her friends and some of her children have passed away already. The structure is the same as ( ex663 ). The only difference is that the speaker uses the recognitional inflected with the characteristic case (`because of that one'). After a short pause, he fills in the referent rirksima `because she respected'. The event `survive' (lit. `jump') and the event `respect' occurred in different times, but they stand in a causal relation.

exe
watik, fi komnzo zathfär bänema fof... nima rirksima brä.\\
watik fi komnzo za thfär bäne=ma fof (.) nima rirk-si=ma b= rä\\
then. only.::: /junp = (.) like.this respect- = =.::: /be\\
`Well, she just lived on because of that... because respected (the taboos). There she is.' tci20120922-26DAK #22-23

exe

In discourse, the use of the recognitional creates some kind of expectation that something should follow. This something can remain empty, for example when the referent is common ground between the speaker and the addressee, but it can also be `filled in' ( ex664 ). This latent expectation explains why the recognitional is employed to introduce another clause ( ex665 ). The function of that clause is determined by the case marker on the recognitional. In ( ex665 ) it is the characteristic case, and consequently the function of the following clause is to mark a reason, in other words bänema can be translated with `because'. The event in the first clause `exit' and the event in the second clause `close' stand in a causal relationship. However, the causal chain of events involves a number of steps.

exe
keke kwamätrakwrm bänema... fam z zwärmänth.\\
keke kwa mätrakwrm bäne=ma (.) fam z zwä rmänth\\::: /exit = (.) thought: >:.::: /close\\
`She did not come outside because they had already closed her thoughts (with magic).' tci20120901-01MAK #148-149
