Lastly, I want to contrast the use of the recognitional from other demonstratives. Consider example ( ex666 ), which includes the general demonstrative ane in the characteristic case in the second clause. The demonstrative ane functions anaphorically, and in that sense it is the mirror image of the recognitional. The events `disturb' and `submerge' stand in a causal relationship, but the components are reversed. We can translate it to English with `therefore' or `that's why'. The two clauses are otherwise independent. This is also supported by the paragraph marker watik `well, then' which occurs at the beginning of the second clause, but this is optional.
summary:
The passage explains that clause combinations can be analyzed using three parameters: verb inflection, how relationships between two fully inflected clauses are marked, and syntactic restrictions within one clause. Nominalized predicates are always subordinate, while clauses with inflected verbs may be classified as coordination or subordination depending on the other parameters; in some cases, only semantic criteria work.

It then shows that Komnzo displays a cline of syntactic integration, especially in causal constructions, ranging from tightly integrated nominalized clauses to more independent clauses linked by demonstratives or case marking. The examples illustrate that stronger semantic connections between events tend to correspond to greater syntactic integration.

text:
exe
ane ŋatha bä nzwathofikwr... watik anema nzibrüzé bobo.\\
ane ŋatha bä nzwa thofikwr (.) watik ane=ma nz=ybrüzé bobo\\
dog: >::: /disturb (.) then = =: >.::: /submerge. \\
`That dog disturbed me there. Well, that's why I pushed him into the water.'\\ tci20130903-03MKW #188

exe

The examples illustrate, that there is a cline between syntactically integrated clauses, i.e. subordinated clauses, and independent clauses. While both ends of the cline are relatively easy to identify, the middle is a grey zone. It is clear that examples like ( ex666 ) consists of two independent clauses. Likewise, the nominalised predicates in ( ex662 - ex664 ) are clear cases of subordination. But examples like ( ex665 ) are somewhat indeterminate. On the one hand, the recognitional pronoun creates a gap that needs to be filled. In other words, semantically, the second clause is subordinated to the first clause. On the other hand, the second clause is syntactically independent. Therefore, I refrain from analysing the recognitional as a subordinator, but rather as having a connecting function. Note that the recognitional demonstrative can be inflected for following cases: characteristic =ma `because', instrumental =me `thereby' and purposive =mr `in order to, until'.

The following description is functionally motivated, that is subsections are sorted thematically. For example, a subsection on purposive clauses will include clear cases of subordination, but also constructions where the purpose is expressed in an independent clause connected with the recognitional. I will describe coordinated clauses ( clausecoordination ), complement clauses ( complementclauses ), adverbial clauses ( advclauses ), relative clauses ( relclauses ), conditional and temporal clauses ( condiclauses ) and direct speech and thought ( directspeechthought ).
summary: The passage argues that there is a continuum between fully subordinated clauses and independent clauses, with some constructions clearly belonging to either end but others forming a grey area. In particular, the recognitional pronoun may create a semantic dependency between clauses, but because the following clause is syntactically independent, it is treated as a connective rather than a subordinator; it can also take case inflections expressing meanings such as ‘because,’ ‘thereby,’ and ‘in order to/until.’ The author says the description will be organized functionally and thematically, covering coordination, complement clauses, adverbial clauses, relative clauses, conditional and temporal clauses, and direct speech/thought.

text:
Coordination refers to syntactic constructions where two or more elements of equal status are connected. Komnzo employs the same mechanisms for coordinating noun phrase s as it does for coordinating clauses. The word a `and' can be used for conjunctive coordination ( ex667 ) and the word o `or' can be used for disjunctive coordination ( ex714 ).

exe
mni wthomonwath a zräföfth.\\
mni w thomonwath a zrä föfth\\
fire: >.::: /prepare.fire and: >.:: /burn\\
`They piled the fire and burn it.' tci20120901-01MAK #155

exe
exe
nafaŋamaf wnfathwr o ynfathwr.\\
nafa-ŋame=f wn fathwr o yn fathwr\\. -mother=.: >.::: /hold or: >.::: /hold\\
`(The child's) mother holds her or holds him.' tci20111004RMA #327-328

exe

For conjunctive coordination it is quite common to have no overt marker ( ex669 ). Especially in sequences of events, two or more inflected verbs can follow each other. Example ( ex669 ) describes the felling of a sago palm.

exe
wati yfarwake... sabthake... safümnzake fof. \\
wati y farwake (.) sa bthake (.) sa fümnzake fof\\
then: >.:: /chop (.): >.:: /finish (.): >.:: /pull.over \\
`Then we chopped it (and) finished it (and) pulled it over.' tci20120929-02SIK #19-21

exe

Other ways of coordinating two clauses involve the manner demonstrative nima `like this', which is commonly used to introduce direct speech ( directspeechthought ). In example ( ex689 ), nima indicates the manner of movement (accompanied by an appropriate gesture), but it also connects the two following clauses.

exe
nabi tutin fä fof zumirwanzrm füsfüsf... nima zfzänzrm fobo... nima zfzänzrm. \\
nabi tuti=n fä fof zu mirwanzrm füsfüs=f (.) nima zf zänzrm fobo (.) nima zf zänzrm\\
bamboo branch=: >.::: /swing wind= (.) like.this: >.::: /carry. (.) like.this: >.::: /carry\\
`The wind was swinging (the lamp) on the bamboo (and) it was moving it there (and) it was moving it here.' tci20111119-03ABB #117-118

exe
summary: Coordination in Komnzo links elements of equal status, and the language uses the same devices for coordinating noun phrases and clauses. The conjunctive marker is **a** ‘and’ and the disjunctive marker is **o** ‘or’, though conjunctive coordination is often unmarked, especially in sequences of events with multiple inflected verbs. Another coordination strategy uses the manner demonstrative **nima** ‘like this’, which can introduce direct speech and also connect clauses.

text:
The most common complement taking predicates in Komnzo are the two phasal verbs thkäfksi `start' and bthaksi `finish'. Other verbs show similar behaviour, for example gathiksi `stop, leave', mäyogsi `continue, repeat'.

With phasal verbs, the indexation structure from the nominalised verb is raised into the matrix clause. The values of those categories expressed in the verb form are marked on the phasal verb. This may include number, person and gender of the arguments, but also tense, aspect, mood and direction. Example ( ex670 ) shows the `non-phasal' clause bad wtharinzake `we were digging the ground'. The verb indexes the actor  and the undergoer bad `ground' (. ). In the first clause of the example, the same state of affairs is expressed, but the verb `dig' occurs in its infinitive tharisi, and its argument structure is raised into the phasal verb thkäfksi `start'. Now it is the phasal verb which indexes a first plural actor and a third singular feminine undergoer.

exe
watik bad fof tharisi zathkäfake... bad wtharinzake zabthake. \\
watik bad fof thari-si za thkäfake (.) bad w tharinzake za bthake\\
then ground dig-: >.::: /start (.) ground: >.::: /dig: >.::: /start\\
`Then we started to dig the ground. We were digging the ground and finished it.'\\ tci20120929-02SIK #72-73

exe

This is also found with ditransitive events, as in ( ex671 ). The verb thkäfksi `start' indexes the indirect object. Note that the dative noun phrase is omitted.

exe
wri no n säthkäfath yarisi. \\
wri no n sä thkäfath yari-si\\
drunk water: >.::: /start give- \\
`They were about to give him alcohol.' tci20120925MAE #158

exe

Verbs in the middle template also raise their respective indexation into the phasal verb. The middle template can be used with several functions ( middletemplatesubsection ). Example ( ex674 ) shows the verb yonasi `drink', which always occurs in a middle template. In the example, yonasi occurs in the infinitive. Consequently, the phasal verb takes over this indexing pattern and only encodes the subject, but not the object.

exe
nä kayé... watik yonasi zethkäfa. \\
nä kayé (.) watik yona-si ze thkäfa\\
some day (.) then drink-::: /start\\
`One day, he started to drink.' tci20120925MAE #83

exe

In example ( ex672 ), the prefixing verb msaksi `sit, dwell' is used in its infinitive. Since, the phasal verb thkäfksi `start' cannot enter the prefixing template, the middle template is used instead. As I describe in prefixingverbsec, the prefixing template is a minor pattern in Komnzo and most intransitive verbs are encoded using the middle template. Furthermore, the prefixing template usually has stative semantics.

exe
wati foba msaksi fefe zathkäfake. \\
wati foba msak-si fefe za thkäfake\\
then. dwell- really::: /start\\
`From there, we began our married life.' (lit. `We began dwelling.')\\ tci20130823-08WAM #47

exe

Example ( ex673 ) shows that for the middle verb yak `run', the phasal verb takes over the indexation. This verb is irregular: instead of a nominalised infinitive with -si, the third singular masculine form yak is used. However, yak is the third singular of `walk' and not of `run'. This would be ŋakwir. Thus, `walk' employs the noun moth `path, way' as its nominalisation and `run' employs yak. Note that the directional value  is also raised into the phasal verb.

exe
kabe ane zenthkäfath yak. \\
kabe ane zen thkäfath yak\\
man:::: /start run\\
`The people started to run here.' tci20131013-01ABB #91

exe
summary: In Komnzo, the most common complement-taking predicates are the phasal verbs *thkäfksi* ‘start’ and *bthaksi* ‘finish’, and these verbs raise the indexation structure of a nominalised complement into the matrix clause. As a result, the phasal verb carries the person, number, gender, tense, aspect, mood, and directional markings that would otherwise belong to the subordinate verb, including in transitive and ditransitive clauses. The same raising applies to verbs in the middle template, and when a prefixing verb is complemented, the middle template is used because the phasal verb cannot take the prefixing template.

text:
Complements of knowledge are structured differently from phasal complements. They involve a property noun with predicative function plus the copula to form a predicate of knowledge ( miyatha `knowledge(-able)') or ignorance ( miyamr `ignorant/ignorance'). Note that the latter has probably developed from a more overt marking that involved the privative case marker =mär. The acquisition of knowledge is expressed by the property noun miyatha plus the light verb ko- `become'. The epistemic content of these predicates of knowledge and ignorance what is known or not known can be expressed by a number of different strategies. Examples ( ex675 ) and ( ex676 ) show complements in which a nominalised verb form in the absolutive is added. In ( ex675 ), the nominalised verb constitutes the head of a compound `coconut climbing'.

exe
nzä miyatha worä ŋazi sogsi. \\
nzä miyatha wo rä ŋazi sog-si\\. knowledge::: /be coconut climb- \\
`I know how to climbing coconut.' (lit. `I am knowledgeable (about) coconut climbing') 1pt [overheard]

exe

The predicate of knowledge construction ( miyatha / miyamr plus copula) is a frequent collocation. Therefore, it is possible to drop the copula altogether, as in ( ex675 ).

exe
bäne ruga yfränzre... afa fi miyamr ykwasi... nzefénzo. \\
bäne ruga y fränzre (.) afa fi miyamr ykwa-si (.) nzefé=nzo\\: pig: >.:: /singe.off (.) father. ignorance cut.meat- (.).. = \\
`We burn the hair off that pig... father doesn't know how to cut it... only I (know).' tci20120821-02LNA #61-62

exe

As described in charcase, the characteristic case can express a topic of conversation. Example ( ex677 ) shows that the epistemic content can also be marked with the characteristic case.

exe
zf wthkärwé zokwasi nzä monme miyatha worä no kzima. \\
zf w thkärwé zokwasi nzä mon=me miyatha wo rä no kzi=ma\\: >.::: /start speech. how= knowledge::: /be rain barktray= \\
`I will start the story how I know about the rain making (magic).'\\ tci20110810-01MAB #8

exe

The epistemic content can be expressed as a relative clause, which takes the predicate of knowledge as its head, as in example ( ex678 ).

exe
bä z miyatha erä maf n zwämg? \\
bä z miyatha e rä maf n zwä mg\\. knowledge::: /be who.: >::: /shoot\\
`Do you know who almost shot me?' tci20130927-06MAB #37

exe

The epistemic content can also be expressed in an independent clause, connected, for example, with nima `like this' ( ex679 ). The use of nima in this example can also be analysed as quoting inner thought ( directspeechthought ).

exe
fi miyamr sfrärm nima fi zbo ern. \\
fi miyamr sf rärm nima fi zbo e rn\\. ignorance.:: /be like.this..::: /be\\
`He did not know those two here.' tci20130927-06MAB #123

exe

The acquisition of knowledge is expressed by replacing the copula with the light verb ko- `become'. Example ( ex680 ) is taken from a text about a punitive custom, whereby the perpetrator is humiliated by being given a large amount of yams, which he is expected to pay back the following year. The epistemic content is expressed by a relative clause.

exe
``miyatha käkor bä monwä zbrigwé bä ra nrä? daw kabe?'' nima kwakonzrmth. \\
miyatha kä kor bä mon=wä z brigwé bä ra n rä daw kabe nima kwa konzrmth\\
knowledge::: /become. how=: >.::: /return. what::: /be garden man::: /say\\
```You see how you pay this back! What are you? A gardener?'' that is what they were saying.' tci20120805-01ABB #241

exe

Note that the phrase miyatha käkor! can be purely epistemic ``(Now) you know it!'' or it can express an experiential sensation ``(Now) you feel it!''.
summary: Complements of knowledge are formed differently from phasal complements: they use a property noun with the copula to make predicates meaning ‘know/knowledge’ (*miyatha*) or ‘be ignorant/ignorance’ (*miyamr*), with acquisition of knowledge expressed by *miyatha* plus the light verb *ko-* ‘become’. The epistemic content can be expressed in several ways, including nominalized verb forms, characteristic case marking, relative clauses, or independent clauses linked by *nima* ‘like this’, and the copula may be omitted because the construction is frequent. The phrase *miyatha käkor!* can mean either ‘Now you know it!’ or ‘Now you feel it!’.

text:
Much of what has been said about complements of knowledge, can be said about complements of desire. The property noun miyo `desire' is used for this. Note that miyo can also be a noun meaning `wish' and `taste'. It can be negated with the privative case =mär: miyomär. Again, a property noun plus copula construction expresses the concept of `want, wish or hope': ra miyo erä? `What do you want' (lit. `What desire you are?'). The clause encoding the desired (or undesired) can be expressed in a variety of ways. Example ( ex681 ) shows a nominalised verb mgthksi `feed' in the absolutive. The verb is heading a compound `pig feeding'.

exe
zena keke miyo worä ruga mgthksi... znsä ttüfr. \\
zena keke miyo wo rä ruga mgthk-si (.) znsä t-tüfr\\
today desire::: /be pig feed- (.) work -plenty\\
`Today, I do not want to feed pigs... too much work.' (lit. `I am not desirous for pig feeding') tci20120805-01ABB #819-820

exe

In example ( ex682 ), the word zokwasi is used as a nominalisation `speaking'.

exe
keke zokwasi miyo nzä worärm yoganai worärm. \\
keke zokwasi miyo nzä wo rärm yoganai wo rärm\\
speech desire.::: /be tired::: /be\\
`I did not want to talk. I was tired.' tci20120922-24MAA #78

exe

The property noun miyo can also be used without the copula, as in ( ex683 ).

exe
frzsi miyomäre fthé kafara znfonzo kerafith thämther. sayäfianme rifthzsi fath zn rä. \\
frz-si miyo=märe fthé kafara zn=fo=nzo ke rafith thä mther sayäfi=anme rifthz-si fath zn rä\\
net- desire= when river pandanus place= =::: /paddle: >::: /lift.up river.crayfish=. hide- place place.::: /be\\
`If you don't want to catch by net, you can paddle to the river pandanus and lift up (the leaves). It is crayfish's hiding place.' tci20130907-02RNA #450-451

exe

The desired proposition can also be expressed in an independent clause which is only semantically connected to the desiderative proposition. In example ( ex684 ), a man threatens a young boy who shot an arrow at him.

exe
zbo z fefe saththma ``nzä fthé miyo kwrarä zena zf mr kwa nwänzé.'' \\
zbo z fefe sa ththma nzä fthé miyo kwra rä zena zf mr kwa n wänzé\\. really: >,::: /stick.on. when desire::: /be today neck: >::: /crack\\
`He stuck (the gun) right at him (saying): ``If I wanted I could breack your neck right here and now.''' tci20130927-06MAB #45

exe
summary: The passage explains that complements of desire, like complements of knowledge, are commonly expressed with the property noun **miyo** ‘desire’ (also ‘wish’ or ‘taste’), which can be negated with the privative case **=mär**. A property-noun-plus-copula construction expresses meanings like ‘want,’ ‘wish,’ or ‘hope,’ while the desired proposition may appear as a nominalized verb, a nominalization such as ‘speaking,’ or even as a separate but semantically linked clause.

text: Adverbial clauses show a wide range of possible constructions. These range from infinitival adjuncts to independent clauses. In the following section, purposive, temporal and manner adverbial clauses are described. Note that the domain of cause was used to introduce the reader to the various levels of syntactic intregration of two clauses. Therefore, I will not discuss this domain here, but refer to interclausintro.
summary: Adverbial clauses can take many forms, ranging from infinitival adjuncts to independent clauses. The passage announces that the following discussion will cover purposive, temporal, and manner adverbial clauses, while cause is not treated here because it was already used to illustrate different degrees of syntactic integration between clauses.

text:
Purposive adverbials are found in different construction. Example ( ex698 ) is from a procedural about making a drum. The speaker explains how a bamboo ring will hold the membrane in place after it is glued to the drum.

exe
nabi riwariwa kwa wäfiyokwre... narsir fof.\\
nabi riwariwa kwa wä fiyokwre (.) nar-si=r fof\\
bamboo ring: >.:: /make (.) press.down- = \\
`We make a bamboo ring... for pressing down (the membrane).'\\ tci20120824KAA #87-88

exe

In example ( ex699 ), the speaker shows me a particular tree used for poison-root fishing. The example shows that the purposive clause can take an object by forming a compound `for swamp poisoning' > `to poison the swamp'. Note that the recognitional pronoun is used just before the nominalised verb.

exe
nä kayé zane zf yirwre bänemr... zra rsrsir.\\
nä kayé zane zf y rwre bänemr (.) zra rsr-si=r\\
day:: >.::: /scrape. (.) swamp poison.fishing- = \\
`Sometimes, we scrape (the root of) this one here for poisoning the waterholes.'\\ tci20130907-02RNA #340

exe

Purposive clauses can also be less syntactically integrated and form an independent clause. In this case, they are usually introduced by the recognitional flagged with purposive case bänemr, which I translate with `in order to'. Example ( ex700 ) describes a tall structure used to show off the amount of a group's yams harvest. This structure involved a long post around which many layers of yam tubers were tied with thick rope.

exe
wati far ane thden sfräzrmth bänemr kwim ŋadme sfmthzgwrmth.\\
wati far ane thd=en sf räzrmth bänemr kwim ŋad=me sf mthzgwrmth\\
then post middle=: >.::: /erect. kwim rope=: >.::: /encircle\\
`Then, they were erecting a post in the middle in order to wrap around the kwim (Acacia mangium) rope.' tci20120805-01ABB #463

exe
summary: Purposive adverbials occur in several constructions. They can appear in a procedural description as a purpose phrase, can form a compound with an object in a nominalized purposive clause, or can occur as a less tightly integrated independent clause introduced by the purposive case marker bänemr, glossed as “in order to.”

text:
Temporal adverbials are found in a number of constructions. Example ( ex690 ) shows the locative case attached to a nominalised verb. The clause ane yam fiyoksin `doing that' is therefore subordinated to the matrix clause. The relation between the two clauses is one of simultaneity.

exe
bäne zrazänzr... fenz kzikaf... mä ke kwa kabef sremar ane yam fiyoksin.\\
bäne zra zänzr (.) fenz kzi=kaf (.) mä keke kwa kabe=f sre mar ane yam fiyok-si=n\\.: >.::: /carry (.) body liquid barktray= (.) where man=.: >.::: /see event make- = \\
`He will carry that one... the body liquid with the barktray... where no man will see him while doing that.' tci20130903-04RNA #49-52

exe

In order to connecting more independent clauses, the word fthé `if, when' is used. This is further described in condiclauses together with conditional clause. A close temporal connection between the two clauses can be established by the word fthémäsü `meanwhile, during'. The words fthé and fthémäsü are historically related, but the etymology of the mäsü part is unclear. In example ( ex691 ), the speaker talks about a particular tree which flowers during the planting season. Note that the first and last clause contain fthé and the middle clause contains fthémäsü: `when X, while Y, that is when Z'.

exe
efthar fthé kräkor minzü... fthémäsü wawa worsi threthkäfth... nzram fthé fof kwa ŋarär.\\
efthar fthé krä kor minzü (.) fthémäsü wawa wor-si thre thkäfth (.) nzram fthé fof kwa ŋa rär\\
dry season when::: /become very (.) meanwhile yam plant-: >::: /start (.) flower when::: /do\\
`When it reaches the height of the dry season... while they are starting to plant the yams... that is when this one will flower.' tci20130907-02JAA #220-221

exe

Fthémäsü is not a subordinator because it can be used on independent clauses with the translation `in the meantime'. In example ( ex692 ), the speaker explains that after his father's death, the stones for rain-making were lost.

exe
nzenme ŋafe fthémäsü kwosi yara... watik foba ni miyamr nrä mafadben zena ethn.\\
nzenme ŋafe fthémäsü kwosi ya ra (.) watik foba ni miyamr n rä mafa=dben zena e thn\\. father meanwhile dead.::: /be (.) then. ignorance::: /be who=.. today::: /lie.down\\
`In the meantime our father died... and from then one we don't know with whom (the rain stones) are today.' tci20131013-01ABB #399

exe

A third strategy to connect a clause temporally is by using the recognitional inflected with the locative case bafen. But this is an infrequent strategy because (i) the temporal function is an extension of the locative case and (ii) connecting clauses is only one function of the recognitional. Example ( ex693 ) is about two men from Rouku who used to work on the Fly River. They run into another man from Rouku, who has been away for a long time. The recognitional occurs twice. First, is it coreferential with holiday: `in that time... during the holidays'. The second use is difficult to analyse because this is also a temporal / conditional construction, but one can assume that bafen introduces the second clause.

exe
fthé nima bafen kabrigrnoth holidayen bafen fefe katrife ``fi bobo yé!'' \\
fthé nima baf=en ka brigrnoth holiday=en baf=en fefe ka trife fi bobo yé\\
when like.this =:::: /return holiday= = really::: /tell...::: /be\\
`When you return in the holidays, then you have say: ``He is there!'''\\ tci20130927-06MAB #206

exe
summary:
The passage describes several ways temporal adverbial clauses are formed. A nominalised verb with locative case can subordinate a clause to express simultaneity, while the words **fthé** ‘if, when’ and **fthémäsü** ‘meanwhile, during’ connect clauses temporally, with **fthémäsü** able to appear in independent clauses and therefore not functioning as a subordinator.

A third, less common strategy uses the recognitional with the locative case **bafen** to link clauses in time. This use is infrequent because its temporal meaning extends from the locative and because the recognitional serves other functions as well.

text:
The proprietive and instrumental case on a nominalised verb can be used to express a manner adverbial clause. In the functional extension, the two case markers can also express a relation of association and temporal overlaps respectively. Hence, the nominalised verb flagged with the proprietive case in example ( ex694 ) can be translated as `He held hips while rejoicing' or `He held hips rejoicingly.'

exe
thweksikarä gon z zefaf.\\
thwek-si=karä gon z ze faf\\
rejoice- = hip::: /hold\\
`He held hips while rejoicing' or `He held hips rejoicingly.' tci20111004RMA #174

exe

The recognitional case also serves to introduce a clause which expresses a manner (or temporal association). In example ( ex695 ), the speaker explains how he and his friends were loading a heavy sago stem on a canoe. Some people from Morehead Station were sceptical about this plan. Thus, bäneme thfkogrm `They were standing with/like this' connects to the following clause which expresses `They stood thinking...'.

exe
nä station kabe fä zämosirath bäneme thfkogrm... fam kwarärmth ``kwa ywokrakwr o kwa ŋabrüzr?'' \\
nä station kabe fä zä mosirath bäne=me thf kogrm (.) fam kwa rärmth kwa y wokrakwr o kwa ŋa brüzr\\
station man::: /gather =::: /stand (.) thought::: /do.::: /float or::: /submerge\\
`Some station people gathered there. They were standing thinking: ``Will it float or will it sink?''' tci20120929-02SIK #30-31

exe

The most common way to encode a manner adverbial is by a relative clause with mon or monme `how' ( relclauses ). Example ( ex696 ) is taken from a picture task, where the participants were asked to arrange picture cards into a story. In the example, the speaker explains the task to a bystander. Note that the recognitional bäneme `with this, in this way' also appears in the first clause. The second recognitional bäne refers to trikasi `story' as we can see in the last clause.

exe
zena ane bäneme nzezinakwre monme bäne wyak brä... trikasi monme kma zrarä.\\
zena ane bäne=me nz=e zinakwre mon=me bäne w yak b= rä (.) trik-si mon=me kma zra rä\\
now = =: >::: /put.down how=..::: /walk =.::: /be (.) tell- how=.::: /be\\
`Now we are putting (the pictures) down how it goes there... how the story should be.' tci20111004RMA #313-314

exe
summary: The passage explains that nominalised verbs marked with the proprietive or instrumental case can express manner adverbial clauses, and these markers may also extend to indicate association or temporal overlap. It also notes that the recognitional case can introduce manner or temporal-association clauses, while the most common strategy for manner adverbials is a relative clause with *mon* or *monme* ‘how’.

text:
I follow Andrews ( Andrews:2007relclauses) in defining relative clauses as a ``subordinate clause which delimits the reference of an NP by specifying the role of the referent of that NP in the situation described by the rc [ relative clause ]''. I adopt Andrews' label NP mat or matrix NP for the NP in the matrix clause, and NP rel for the NP in the relative clause. The latter is always expressed by interrogative pronouns, which function as relative pronouns. Hence, Komnzo and other Yam languages employ the ``relative pronoun strategy'' for relativisation, which from a cross-linguistic perspective is found mostly in Europe.

Relative clauses in Komnzo are adjoined clauses in the sense of Hale ( Hale:1976adjoined), who notes that adjoined relative clauses are ``subordinate in some way, but [their] surface position with respect to the main clause is marginal rather than embedded'' ( Hale:1976adjoined). Andrews defines them as having the relative clause appear outside the matrix NP. Relative clauses in Komnzo are almost always right-adjoined, i.e. they follow the matrix NP. Alternatively, they may refer to the whole preceding (matrix) clause. The matrix NP can be fronted together with the relative clause, which is a common strategy used for topicalisation ( info-cleft ).

We can represent the structure of relative clauses schematically, as in Figure relclause. The matrix element, [...] mat in the figure, is usually a noun phrase, which can be omitted if it is understood from context. Alternatively, the matrix element can be a matrix clause. The relative clause, [...] rc in the figure, consists of the relative pronoun and the verb. There may be one noun phrase preceding the relative pronoun, but there cannot be more than one noun phrase in this position.

I begin by describing the formal structure of relative clauses. Formally, they are similar to content questions because the relative pronouns are identical to the interrogative pronouns. I refer the reader to interrogatives-sec for a description of interrogative pronouns. See especially interrogatives-table, but also the interrogatives in demonstratives-table. We could say that interrogatives function as relative pronouns, which is why I do not gloss them as rel in the following examples. Instead, I gloss them in the same manner, in which pronouns in interrogative function are glossed. However, relative clauses are semantically distinct from content questions because the answer to the question is already given in the form of the NP mat. Relative clauses are also syntactically different from content questions in that the relative pronoun has to occur as the second element ( relclause ). Such a restriction does not apply to content questions. This is illustrated in ( ex541 - ex543 ), where the relative clause in each example is printed in bold face.

Example ( ex541 ) comes from a hunting story where the narrator had encountered a spirit which began chasing him. In the example, the relative pronoun maf follows the pronoun nzä. The relative clause follows the NP mat ane kabe `that man'.

exe
nze nima ``byannor ane kabe fof nzä maf wonrsoknwr.''\\
nze nima b=yan nor ane kabe fof nzä maf won rsoknwr\\. =.:::: /shout man. who..: >:::: /bother\\
`I said: ``He is shouting out there. This man who bothers me.'''\\ tci20111119-03ABB #164-166

exe

In example ( ex542 ), the speaker describes why he did not pay attention to a fire that almost burned his garden. In the example, the relative pronoun mane is preceded by the noun phrase mnz tharthar `side of the house'. This is an adjoined relative clause because it is outside the NP mat, which in this case is mni `fire', whose antecedent is understood from the context.

exe
ni fi ane zumarwrme mnz thartharen mane zfrärm.\\
ni fi ane zu marwrme mnz tharthar=en mane zf rärm\\
but: >.::: /look house side= which.::: /be\\
`But we were looking at that (fire), which was on the side of the house.'\\ tci20120922-24STK #5

exe

Finally, in ( ex543 ) the speaker describes how he was trying to remove a burning tree from his garden fence. The relative pronoun mane follows the ergative marked wämne `tree'. This is an adjoined relative clause because it is outside the matrix NP, which in this case is ŋarake `garden fence', whose antecedent is understood from the context.

exe
kma wämne ane fof kwakarkwé ane fof wämnef mane thänarfa... keke watikthémäre.\\
kma wämne ane fof kwa karkwé ane fof wämne=f mane thä narfa (.) keke watik-thé=märe\\
tree::: /pull tree= which: >::: /press.down (.) enough- = \\
`I should have pulled that tree (from the fence), which the tree was pushing down. No, (I was) not (strong) enough!' tci20120922-24MAA #42-43

exe

A second rule is needed for examples where the relative pronoun occurs in initial position of the relative clause. Although this is possible, such examples are much less frequent than the second position. The relative pronoun can occur in first position only (i) if it is preceded by the NP mat ( ex544 and ex545 ), or (ii) if the only other element in the relative clause is the verb ( ex546 ).

exe
bundbonzo rä mane zawokth.\\
bundbo=nzo rä mane za wokth\\. =.:: /be which::: /choose\\
`It is up to you which one you choose!' tci20111004RMA #528

exe

Example ( ex544 ) is taken from a picture stimulus task. One of the participants is correcting the other. Note that the English translation is misleading. The noun phrase mafanemäwä waniwani is a complex noun phrase and the relative pronoun mafanema is marked flagged with the characteristic case in adnominal function. Thus, mafanemäwä waniwani should be translated not as genitive `whose picture', but as origin `picture of/about who'.
summary:
The passage defines Komnzo relative clauses as subordinate clauses that limit the reference of a matrix NP by specifying the role of its referent in the relative clause, and notes that Komnzo uses a relative-pronoun strategy with interrogative pronouns serving as relative pronouns. These clauses are typically adjoined and right-adjoined after the matrix NP, though they can also refer to an entire preceding matrix clause or be fronted with the matrix NP for topicalization.  

Formally, Komnzo relative clauses resemble content questions because they use the same pronouns, but they differ semantically because the referent is already supplied by the matrix NP and syntactically because the relative pronoun must usually be the second element in the clause. Initial-position relative pronouns are possible but less common, and only under restricted conditions.

text:
exe
sukawi, nima keke rä. zane fthéthamane yé... ane kabe fof mafanemäwä waniwani zöbthé nzünmarwre.\\

`Sukawi, it is not like that. This is from that time... really this man whose picture we just saw before.' tci20111004RMA #194

In example ( ex545 ), the relative pronoun occurs initially following the NP mat dödö.

exe
ane fathnzo zfrärm wämne keke... dödönzo... dödö maneme ŋarenwre fath.\\
ane fath=nzo zf rärm wämne keke (.) dödö=nzo (.) dödö mane=me ŋa renwre fath\\

`This was a clearing, no trees... only dödö (Sida acuta)... dödö, with which we sweep the clear places.' tci20120821-02LNA #25-27

Next, I describe which kinds of argument roles can be relativised in the matrix clause (NP mat ), and which can occur in the relative clause (NP rel ). As the examples in this section show, there is virtually no restriction on the possible argument roles. NP rel is expressed by the relative pronoun, which can inflect for all cases ( interrogatives-sec ). The examples given in this section include the following cases: ergative ( ex541 ), absolutive ( ex542, ex543, ex546 ), characteristic ( ex544 ), dative ( ex551 ), locative ( ex547 ), and instrumental ( ex545 ).

It is harder to determine the argument role of NP mat because its presence is optional. We saw in ( ex543 ) that the relative pronoun mane referred to the fence, which the burning tree had pushed down. But this is not expressed by a noun phrase, nor is the fence indexed in the verb of the matrix clause. We only know about it from the preceding context of the story, and the plural prefix in the verb of the relative clause. The word ŋarake `fence' is frequently used in the plural. In ( ex542 ), the fire is not expressed as a noun phrase, but the prefix of the verbs zumarwrme `we were seeing it' and zfrärm `it was', both indexing mni `fire' (3. ). However, we can always determine the argument role of NP mat from the context. The following argument roles are found in the examples given in this section: the single argument of an intransitive verb ( ex541 ), patient ( ex542 ), location ( ex547 ), discourse topic ( ex548 ), actor ( ex549 ), and recipient ( ex550 ).

exe
mni wthomonwrth yfö mä zfrärm.\\
mni w thomonwrth yfö mä zf rärm\\
fire: >.::: /pile.up.fire hole where.::: \\
`They prepare the fire where the hole was.' tci20120901-01MAK #153-154

`This was another small story like this... about my small matches... about the fire, which they were calling Kidn or base fire before.' tci20120909-06KAB #126-127

It is also possible that the relative clause is free in the sense that it refers to the whole matrix clause and not to a particular nominal. Examples are given in ( ex546 ) and ( ex551 ).

exe
be fam kwot karäré tosin mafan kwa yarithr.\\
be fam kwot ka räré tosin mafan kwa ya rithr\\. thought properly::: /do torch who..: >.::: /give\\
`You have to think properly to whom you will give the torch.' 1pt [overheard]

exe

The NP mat can be fronted together with the relative clause, as in ( ex556 ). This is commonly used for topicalisation. After showing me a traditional fishing basket, the speaker shifts the topic to more modern methods of fishing. The NP mat is net in ( ex556 ).

exe
wati, net ane mane erä markaianeme erä ane.\\
wati net ane mane e rä markai=aneme e rä ane\\

`Okay, as for the fishing nets, they are the white man's (things).'\\ tci20120906SKK #53-54

exe

In example ( ex555 ), the speaker talks about food taboos. He makes the point that a particular woman in the village has grown very old because she has always respected those food taboos. The relative clause (in bold) marks a shift in topic to all those people who did not respect the food taboos. The antecedent of the relative clause is omitted, since it is understood from context. It is different from the old woman, as can been seen by that fact that all following verbs index a plural argument, e.g. kwarirkwrmth `they respected' and thufathwrm `it grabbed them'.

exe
watik, fi komnzo zathfär... bänema fof nima rirksima brä... nima kwarirkwrm... fi mafa keke kwarirkwrmth... watik, tekmär esufakwa kwikkwikf thufathwrm.\\
watik fi komnzo za thfär (.) bäne=ma fof nima rirk-si=ma b= rä (.) nima kwa rirkwrm (.) fi mafa keke kwa rirkwrmth (.) watik tek=mär e sufakwa kwik-kwik=f thu fathwrm\\
then. only.::: /jump (.): = like.this respect- = =.::: /be (.) like.this::: /respect (.) but who..::: /respect (.) then duration=::: /grow.old -sickness=: >::: /hold\\
`She just lives on... because of her respect... she was respecting (the law)... but those who did not respect (the law)... well, they grew old quickly and they got sick.' tci20120922-26DAK #22-27

summary: The passage explains that Zauzou relative clauses are highly flexible: the relative pronoun can inflect for all cases, and virtually any argument role may be relativised in the relative clause, including ergative, absolutive, dative, locative, instrumental, and others. It also notes that the antecedent in the matrix clause is often omitted and recoverable from context, so the relative clause may be free and refer to the whole preceding clause, and the matrix NP can optionally be fronted with the relative clause for topicalisation.

text: The fronted relative clause as a topicalisation strategy is described in detail in info-cleft.
summary: The passage states that the fronted relative clause functions as a topicalization strategy. It also notes that this construction is described in detail in the section on info-cleft.

text:
Conditional and time clauses are expressed in the same way, only the context resolves which of the two is meant. I will use the term conditional in the subsequent description to cover both. Conditionals are formed by using the word fthé `when, if'. Note that fthé is not a subordinator per se because it can also occur in independent sentences with the meaning `that is when'. Thus, fthé is required for a conditional, but it is not sufficient. The word fthé is used in the clause which sets up the conditional, often called the if- clause. The second clause, often called the then- clause, receives no special marking. Note that for time clauses, this would be the when-clause and then-clause respectively. The clearest conditional reading is found with the second person. While an irrealis verb inflection is also possible, in most cases, the imperative is used in one of the two clauses, as in example ( ex646 ) and ( ex647 ).

exe
ŋanzmäre fthé gnräré frasi kwa nrä. \\
ŋanz=märe fthé gn räré frasi kwa n rä\\
row= when::: /be hunger::: /be\\
`If you are without a row (of yams in the garden), you will be hungry.'\\ tci20130822-08LNA #17

exe
exe
wati, zena fthé zanmar... yusi fr mane rä... ane fof nzone farsima rä. \\
wati zena fthé zan mar (.) yusi fr mane rä (.) ane fof nzone far-si=ma rä\\
then today when: >.::: /see (.) grass stem which.::: /be (.). fell- =.::: /be\\
`If/When you look at it... the grassland there... that is from my cutting down (the trees).' tci20120805-01ABB #614

exe

Both clauses can be marked for various TAM categories, for example imperative in the if-clause and irrealis in the when-clause in ( ex648 ), where the speaker shows me the proper use of a toy bullroarer.

exe
zbo fthé sakwr fefen o wämnen... keke kwa srannor. \\
zbo fthé sa kwr fefe=n o wämn=en (.) keke kwa sran nor\\. when: >.::: /hit body= or tree= (.).::: /shout\\
`If you hit it here against the body or against a tree, it will not make a sound.'\\ tci20120914RMA #31-33

exe

In ( ex649 ), all clauses are in past durative, yet the conditional construction can be interpreted as both actual (as in the translation) or counterfactual (`... the story man would have shot them with magic').

exe
zizi zä keke kwarafinzrmth ŋoŋoyamkarä... bänema fthé ŋoŋoyamkarä kwarafinzrmth menzf thfruthrm... bthanme. \\
zizi zä keke kwa rafinzrmth ŋoŋoyam=karä (.) bäne=ma fthé ŋoŋoyam=karä kwa rafinzrmth menz=f thf ruthrm (.) bthan=me\\
afternoon::: /paddle noise=... = when noise=::: /paddle story.man=.: >::: /shoot (.) magic= \\
`They did not paddle her with a lot of noise in the afternoon. If they were paddling making a lot of noise, the story man was shooting them with.'\\ tci20120922-19DAK #14-15

exe
summary: Conditional and time clauses are formed in the same way, with context determining whether the construction means “if” or “when”; the term *conditional* is used to cover both. They are introduced by *fthé* ‘when, if,’ which can also occur independently, so it is necessary but not sufficient for a conditional reading, and the second clause receives no special marking. The clearest conditional meaning appears with second-person reference, and while irrealis marking is possible, imperatives are often used in one of the clauses; both clauses may also carry other TAM markings, allowing some constructions to be interpreted as either actual or counterfactual.

text:
Direct speech is a common construction in Komnzo. In most cases, direct speech is introduced by a speech verb, for example ko- `speak' or na- `say', and the manner demonstrative nima `like this' ( manner-demonstrative-subsec ). Direct speech receives a separate intonation contour and the whole clause is often produced at a slightly higher pitch to indicate that the speaker is taking on another person's role. An example is given in ( ex650 ).

exe

xlist
watik, srank kma sakora nima ``srank, ni krafare!''\\
watik srank kma sa kora nima srank ni kra fare\\
then srank: >.::: /speak srank::: /set.off\\
`Well, he tried to tell Srank: ``Srank, we go!''
srankf zenaftha ``keke efoth zizi fefe rä nzä kayé woräro.''\\
srank=f ze naftha keke efoth zizi fefe rä nzä kayé wo räro\\
srank=.::: /say sun afternoon really.::: /be. tomorrow:::: /be\\
Srank said: ``No, it is late afternoon. I will go tomorrow.'''\\ tci20111107-01MAK #44-45
xlist
exe

The manner demonstrative functions as a quotative marker. It can introduce direct speech without a speech verb, as in example ( ex651 ).

exe
naf nima ``nakre! wimäsen mni bŋasog.''\\
naf nima nakre wimäs=en mni b=ŋa sog\\. nakre mango.tree= fire =::: /climb\\
`He said: ``Nakre! The fire is climbing up the mango tree.'''\\ tci20130901-04RNA #152-153

exe

There is no dedicated construction for indirect speech. Indirect speech equivalents can be expressed by a speech verb with an adverbial adjunct ( ex652 ) or a clause connected with mon `how' ( ex653 ).

exe
naf ŋanafr drdr mäyogsir.\\
naf ŋa nafr drdr mäyog-si=r\\.::: /speak old.garden repeat- = \\
`She said to continue the old garden.' tci20130823-06STK 161

exe
exe
emothf ŋatrikwr monme zfnzr.\\
emoth=f ŋa trikwr mon=me z fnnzr\\
girl=.::: /tell how=: >.::: /hit\\
`The girl reports how he hit her.' tci20120925MAE #102

exe

An individual's inner thoughts are treated like direct and indirect speech. Hence, we find examples like ( ex654 ) and ( ex655 ), which mirror what has been described above for speech. The only difference lies in the framing expression, which is often the light verb construction fam `thought' + rä- `do'.

exe
fam zära ``kar bä rä a kar töna fobo fof wyak fof.'' \\
fam zä ra kar bä rä a kar töna fobo fof w yak fof\\
thought::: /do village.::: /be and place high.ground.::: /walk \\
`He thought ``There is a village. I will walk there to the high ground.'''\\ tci20131013-01ABB #259

exe
exe
fam ane fof ŋarär monme sufnzrmth monme santhbath. \\
fam ane fof ŋa rär mon=me su fnnzrmth mon=me san thbath\\

`He is thinking how they were hitting him and how they locked him up.'\\ tci20111004RMA #457

exe
summary: Direct speech is common in Komnzo and is usually introduced by a speech verb such as *ko-* ‘speak’ or *na-* ‘say’ together with the manner demonstrative *nima* ‘like this’; it has its own intonation contour and is often spoken at a slightly higher pitch to mark the speaker’s adoption of another person’s role. The demonstrative can also function alone as a quotative marker, and there is no special construction for indirect speech, which is instead expressed with a speech verb plus an adverbial adjunct or with a clause linked by *mon* ‘how’. Inner thoughts are treated similarly to speech, with the main difference being the framing expression, often the light verb construction *fam* ‘thought’ plus *rä-* ‘do’.

text: In this chapter the three morphologically marked moods of Fwe are discussed: the imperative in bkm:Ref489881434, the perfective subjunctive in bkm:Ref492309168, and the imperfective subjunctive in bkm:Ref489363941.
summary: The chapter discusses the three morphologically marked moods in Fwe: the imperative, the perfective subjunctive, and the imperfective subjunctive. Each of these moods is treated in a separate section.

text:
An imperative form in Fwe is formed with a suffix -e, but without the subject marker, as in ( bkm:Ref99102804 -- bkm:Ref99102805 ). The imperative form ending in -a, as commonly found in Bantu languages, does not exist in Fwe.

yêndè\\
é̲nd-e\\
go- pfv. sbjv \\
‘Go!’

zwé hànò\\
zw-é̲ hano\\
come_out- pfv. sbjv dem. ii 16 \\
‘Get out of here!’ (ZF_Elic14)

The suffix -e is also used in the perfective subjunctive, which is only distinguished from the imperative form by the presence of the subject marker. The imperative and the perfective subjunctive also take the same melodic tones. When used without an object marker, the imperative takes melodic tone 1, combined with melodic tone 4, the deletion of underlying high tones, as in ( bkm:Ref71903613 -- bkm:Ref74908194 ). (See bkm:Ref71539267 for an overview of melodic tones.) With an object marker, the imperative combines melodic tone 4 with melodic tone 3 instead of melodic tone 1, as in ( bkm:Ref71903625 -- bkm:Ref74908216 ).

hùwé ꜝcáhà\\
huw-é̲ cáha\\
shout- pfv. sbjv very\\
‘Shout loudly.’

kàbìré mùnjûò\\
kabir-é̲ mu-N-júo\\
enter- pfv. sbjv np 18 - np 9 -house\\
‘Enter the house.’ (NF_Elic15)

fùrùmìké kàsúbà kò\\
fu H rumik-é̲ ka-súba ko\\
turn_upside_down- pfv. sbjv np 12 -dish dem. iii 12 \\
‘Turn that dish upside down.’ (NF_Elic17)

bàtúsè\\
ba H -tus-é̲\\
om 2 -help- pfv. sbjv \\
‘Help them.’

ndìàmbîsè\\
ndi-amb-í̲s-e\\
om 1SG -talk- caus - pfv. sbjv \\
‘Talk to me.’ (NF_Elic17)

ndìbèrékèrè\\
ndi-beré̲k-er-e\\
om 1SG -work- appl - pfv. sbjv \\
‘Work for me.’ (NF_Elic15)

The imperative is used to express a command or order. An order expressed with the imperative is considered less polite and more direct than an order expressed with the subjunctive. The imperative can only be used for orders directed at a singular addressee, as in ( bkm:Ref98771149 -- bkm:Ref98771152 ). Orders directed at plural addressees are expressed by subjunctives (see Sections bkm:Ref492309168 - bkm:Ref489363941 ).

íwè tóndè kúnò\\
iwé tó̲nd-e kunó\\
pers 2SG watch- pfv. sbjv dem. ii 17 \\
‘You! Look here!’ (NF_Narr15)

tòntórè\\
to H ntor-é̲\\
be_quiet- pfv. sbjv \\
‘Be quiet!’ (NF_Elic17)

The negation of both the imperative and subjunctive form takes a post-initial prefix ásha-, and a final vowel suffix -i, as well as a different tonal pattern. The negation of imperatives and subjunctives is discussed in bkm:Ref499029715.
summary:
In Fwe, the imperative is formed with the suffix -e and no subject marker; unlike many Bantu languages, it does not have an imperative in -a. The same -e form is also used for the perfective subjunctive, which differs from the imperative only by the presence of a subject marker, and both share the same melodic tone patterns.

The imperative expresses direct commands or orders, is less polite than the subjunctive, and is used only for singular addressees; plural addressees are addressed with subjunctives. Negated imperatives and subjunctives use the prefix ásha-, the final vowel -i, and a different tonal pattern.

text:
The perfective subjunctive form is formed with the suffix -e on the verb, and, unlike the imperative, takes a subject marker. Other than the presence of the subject marker, the perfective subjunctive is identical to the imperative, and also takes the same melodic tones: melodic tone 1 and 4 when the verb lacks an object marker, as in ( bkm:Ref74908272 -- bkm:Ref74908273 ), or 3 and 4 when the verb includes an object marker, as in ( bkm:Ref74908306 -- bkm:Ref74908307 ).

òtùmbùsé mùrìrò\\
o-tu H mbus-é̲ mu-riro\\
sm 2SG -light- pfv. sbjv np 3 -fire\\
‘You should light a fire.’ (ZF_Elic14)

mùbíːkè òtúꜝcényà\\
mu-bí̲ːk-e o-tú-cenyá\\
sm 2PL -put- pfv. sbjv aug - np 13 -small\\
‘You should put a little bit.’ (NF_Elic15)

tùmùbóózèrè ècìntú ꜝcákwè\\
tu-mu-boó̲z-er-e e-ci-ntú cí-akwé\\
sm 1PL - om 1SG -return- appl - sbjv aug - np 7 -thing pp 7 - poss 3SG \\
‘We should bring his thing back to him.’ (ZF_Conv13)

tùzìbbátúrè èzí zìkûnì\\
tu-zi H -bba H t-ú̲r-e e-zí zi-kúni\\
sm 1PL - om 8 -separate- sep. tr - pfv. sbjv aug - dem. i 8 np 8 -tree\\
‘Can we separate these trees?’ (NF_Elic15)

The perfective subjunctive describes a one-time event, as in ( bkm:Ref99102952 ), and contrasts with the imperfective subjunctive, which describes habitual or ongoing events, as in ( bkm:Ref99102971 ) (see also bkm:Ref489884199 ).

òndìtúsè\\
o-ndi-tus-é̲\\
sm 2SG - om 1SG -help- pfv. sbjv \\
‘You should help me (one time only).’

wákùndìtùsà\\
o-áku-ndi-tus-a\\
sm 2SG - sbjv. ipfv - om 1SG -help- fv \\
‘You should help me regularly/be helping me.’ (NF_Elic17)

A near future can be derived from the perfective subjunctive by addition of a future prefix mbo-, and an additional high tone on the subject marker (see bkm:Ref489880945 ).

The perfective subjunctive has various functions. It can express a plan or intention, as in ( bkm:Ref489953824 ), where the speaker discusses what he plans to do to escape a fire.

tùpìcùké mùrìrò tùyé òkò úkàzwîrà\\
tu-pi H cuk-é̲ mu-riro tu-y-é̲ o-ko ú̲-ka-zw-í̲r-a\\
sm 1PL -escape- pfv. sbjv np 3 -fire
sm 1PL -go- pfv. sbjv aug - dem. iii 17 sm 3. rel - dist -come_out- appl - fv \\
‘We will dodge the fire, we will go to where it comes from.’ (NF_Narr17)

The perfective subjunctive can be used to express volition or desire, as in ( bkm:Ref449440622 -- bkm:Ref449440623 ).

nêyè àyéndè nêyè\\
né=ye a-é̲nd-e né=ye\\
com = pers 3SG sm 1 -go- pfv. sbjv com = pers 3SG \\
‘She too wanted to go with her.’ (NF_Narr15)

ndìpátámè\\
ndi-patam-é̲\\
sm 1SG -lie_on_stomach- pfv. sbjv \\
‘I want to lie down a bit.’ (ZF_Elic14)

When combined with the adverb nanga, the perfective subjunctive expresses uncertainty, as in ( bkm:Ref99103032 -- bkm:Ref99103033 ). Note that the adverb nanga with the imperfective subjunctive does not express uncertainty, but immediate future (see bkm:Ref489884199 ).

nàngà bàkéːzyè bàtùpángé cìmwî\\
nanga ba-ké̲ːzy-e ba-tu H -pang-é̲ ci-mwí\\
even sm 2 -come- pfv. sbjv sm 2 - om 1PL -do- pfv. sbjv pp 7 -other\\
‘He might come and do something else to us.’ (NF_Narr15)

wáshàívùkùmì nàngà ìfwê\\
o-ásha-í-vukum-i nanga i-fw-é̲\\
sm 2SG - neg. sbjv - om 9 -throw- neg even sm 9 -die- pfv. sbjv \\
‘Don’t throw it, it might break.’

àndìzìmísìkìzè màláìtì ángù nàngà àndìhìsíkìzè ènjûò\\
a-ndi-zim-í̲sikiz-e ma-láiti nanga a-ndi-his-í̲kiz-e e-N-júo\\
sm 1 - om 1SG -go_out- caus. appl - pfv. sbjv np 6 -light
even sm 6 - om 1SG - caus - appl - pfv. sbjv aug - np 9 -house\\
‘S/he must turn off the lights for me, they might burn down my house.’ (NF_Elic17)

With a first person subject, the perfective subjunctive may express a hortative, as in ( bkm:Ref99103056 -- bkm:Ref99103057 ).

tùràpérè\\
tu-raper-é̲\\
sm 1PL -pray- pfv. sbjv \\
‘Let’s pray.’ (ZF_Elic14)

ndìrìkòshórèkó bùryô\\
ndi-ri H -ko H sh-ó̲r-e=ko bu-ryó\\
sm 1SG - om 5 -cut- sep. tr - pfv. sbjv = loc 17 np 14 -just\\
‘Let me just cut it.’ (ZF_Narr14)

kàntí ndìkùtòmbwérìsè\\
kantí ndi-ku-tombwé̲r-is-e\\
well sm 1SG - om 2SG -weed- caus - pfv. sbjv \\
‘Then let me help you weed.’ (NF_Narr15)

With a second person subject, the subjunctive may express a command, as in ( bkm:Ref99103078 -- bkm:Ref99103080 ).

òkêːzyè òndìtúsè\\
o-ké̲ːzy-e o-ndi-tus-é̲\\
sm 2SG -come- pfv. sbjv sm 2SG - om 1SG -help- pfv. sbjv \\
‘Come and help me.’

mùtòntórè mùyéndè mùkàráːrè\\
mu-to H ntor-é̲ mu-é̲nd-e mu-ka-raː H r-é̲\\
sm 2PL -be_quiet- pfv. sbjv sm 2PL -go- pfv. sbjv sm 2PL - dist -sleep- pfv. sbjv \\
‘Be quiet and go to sleep.’ (NF_Elic15)

A command expressed with the subjunctive form is usually interpreted as more polite than a command expressed with the imperative form (see bkm:Ref489881434 ). To express even more politeness, the prefix ngá- ‘can’ can be added, as in ( bkm:Ref99103146 ).

ngóndìtúsè kùndìkwátìrà ècí cìpùpè\\
ngá-o-ndi-tus-é̲ ku-ndi-kwát-ir-a e-cí ci-pupe \\
can- sm 2SG - om 1SG -help- pfv. sbjv inf - om 1SG -grab- appl - fv
aug - dem. i 7 np 7 -container\\
‘Can you please carry that container for me?’ (ZF_Elic14)

Subjunctives are also used in subordinate clauses, where they can carry the same functions as subjunctives in main clauses, or can be used to express the desired or intended consequence of the event expressed in the main clause, as in ( bkm:Ref99103166 -- bkm:Ref99103168 ).

bàmùbérékérà òkùtéyè àfúmè \\
ba-mu-berek-er-á̲ okuteye a-fum-é̲\\
sm 2 - om 1 -work- fv that sm 1 -become_rich- pfv. sbjv \\
‘They work for him, so that he becomes rich.’ (NF_Elic17)

mbóshàkèsháké àkàshérêŋì òpàngé àkà-business\\
mbo-ó̲-shake-shak-é̲ a-ka-sheréŋi o-pang-é̲ a-ka-business \\
near. fut - sm 2SG - pl 2-find- pfv. sbjv aug - np 12 -money
sm 2SG -make- pfv. sbjv aug - np 12 -business\\
‘You will find a little money so that you make a small business.’ (ZF_Conv13)
summary:
The perfective subjunctive is formed with the suffix -e and, unlike the imperative, includes a subject marker; apart from that, it matches the imperative in form and melodic tones, with different tone patterns depending on whether an object marker is present. It denotes a one-time event rather than habitual or ongoing action, and can express a range of functions including plans, intentions, desire, uncertainty with nanga, hortative meanings with first-person subjects, and polite commands with second-person subjects.  

Subjunctives also occur in subordinate clauses, where they may have the same uses as in main clauses or express a desired or intended result of the main clause. A near future form can be created by adding the future prefix mbo- and an extra high tone on the subject marker.

text:
The perfective subjunctive can combine with the remoteness prefix na-; in subordinate clauses, this indicates a remote future, as in ( bkm:Ref74908458 -- bkm:Ref74908459 ). In main clauses, the perfective subjunctive with na- expresses the same functions as the perfective subjunctive without na-, only set in the remote future, such as a command to be followed up tomorrow, not today. This use is illustrated in ( bkm:Ref74908501 -- bkm:Ref74908502 ). Remoteness is usually considered as at least one day removed from the day of speaking, as it is throughout the tense/aspect system of Fwe (see, for instance, the remote past perfective, bkm:Ref489260766 ).

mbùtí náyìwánè èyí shérêŋì\\
N-bu-tí na-á̲-i H -wan-é̲ e-í ∅-sheréŋi\\
cop - np 14 -how rem - sm 1 - om 9 -find- pfv. sbjv aug - dem. i 9 np 9 -money\\
‘How will he get this money?’ (Lit.: ‘It is how that he will get this money?’) (ZF_Conv13)

éwè zyúmùnyà ndíwè nóbè háꜝkátì\\
éwe zyú-munya ndí-we na-ó̲-b-e há-ka-tí\\
pers 2SG pp 1 -other
cop - pers 2SG rem - sm 2SG -be- pfv. sbjv np 16 - np 12 -middle\\
‘You, the other one, it is you who will be in the middle.’ (ZF_Narr13)

nóyêndè zyônà\\
na-ó̲-é̲nd-e zyóna\\
rem - sm 2SG -go- pfv. sbjv tomorrow\\
‘Go tomorrow.’

nìbézyè bàkùbónè\\
ni-bá̲-izy-e ba-ku-bo H n-é̲\\
rem - sm 2SG -come- pfv. sbjv sm 2 - om 2SG -see- pfv. sbjv \\
‘She has to come and take care of you.’ (NF_Narr17)

The remoteness prefix na- is used with the verb ta ‘say’ in the subjunctive, followed by a subjunctive main verb, to express an event that almost, but not quite, took place, as in ( bkm:Ref99103237 -- bkm:Ref99103238 ).

nàté ndìmùcáîsè zywínà\\
na-ta-é̲ ndi-mu-caí̲s-e zwiná\\
rem -say- pfv. sbjv sm 1SG - om 1 -bump_into- pfv. sbjv dem. iv 1 \\
‘I almost bumped into her/him, that one.’ (NF_Elic17)

nòbónì cwárè rìn’ éòndè nàté òírè\\
no-bón-i cwaré riná e-∅-onde na-ta-é o-ir-é̲ \\
sm 2SG. pst -see- npst. pfv then dem. iv 5 aug - np 5 -waterlily
rem -say- pfv. sbjv sm 2SG -go. appl - pfv. sbjv \\
‘Did you see that flower that you wanted to go to?’ (Context: a boy wanted to pick a waterlily. A bird warns him not to, picks up the waterlily and reveals a snake underneath it. The bird returns to the boy and discusses what would have happened if he went to pick the waterlily as he planned.) (NF_Narr17)
summary:
The perfective subjunctive can combine with the remoteness prefix **na-**, and in subordinate clauses this marks a **remote future**. In main clauses, it has the same meanings as the perfective subjunctive without **na-**, but with the event placed in the remote future, usually understood as at least one day away from the day of speaking.

The prefix **na-** is also used with **ta** ‘say’ in the subjunctive, followed by a subjunctive main verb, to express an event that **almost happened** but did not quite take place.

text:
An imperfective subjunctive is formed with the post-initial prefix áku-, as in ( bkm:Ref99103273 ). Verbs in the imperfective subjunctive maintain their underlying tones, and aside from the high tone associated with the prefix áku- itself, no melodic high tones are added.

ènwé ꜝbáꜝnángù mwákùkàrà\\
enwé bá-na-angú mu-áku-kar-a\\
pers 2PL np 2 -child- poss 1SG sm 2PL - sbjv. ipfv -stay- fv \\
‘You, my children, must stay here.’ (NF_Elic17)

The second syllable ku of the prefix áku- is derived from the infinitive prefix ku-. Two of the characteristics of the imperfective subjunctive point to its origin in an infinitive: the fact that the syllable ku may change to ka when used with the distal marker (see ( bkm:Ref490842863 )), and the lack of melodic tones, which is typical of infinitives and rarely seen in inflected verbs (see also bkm:Ref71540393 ).

Habitual is a subtype of imperfective aspect, and the imperfective subjunctive is therefore often used with a habitual meaning, combined with the habitual suffix -ang, as in ( bkm:Ref99103335 ) (see also bkm:Ref451268511 ).

wákùmùtùsàngà\\
o-áku-mu-tus-ang-a\\
sm 2SG - sbjv. ipfv - om 1 -help- hab - fv \\
‘You should help her/him regularly.’ (NF_Elic17)

Without the habitual suffix -ang, both a habitual and a progressive reading are possible, as in ( bkm:Ref99103358 ). The imperfective subjunctive does not combine with overt progressive markers, and in most cases, such as in ( bkm:Ref99103360 ), the habitual reading appears to be preferred.

wákùmùtùsà\\
o-áku-mu-tus-a\\
sm 2SG - sbjv. ipfv - om 1 -help- fv \\
‘You should be helping her/him.’ / ‘You should help her/him regularly.’

wákùmùtùsàngà\\
o-áku-mu-tus-ang-a\\
sm 2SG - sbjv. ipfv - om 1 -help- hab - fv \\
‘You should help her/him regularly.’ (NF_Elic17)

From the imperfective subjunctive, a near future imperfective is derived by addition of the prefix mbo-, see bkm:Ref490749852.

More data are needed to study the range of meanings of the imperfective subjunctive, though it appears to be similar to that of the perfective subjunctive, e.g. a command, as in ( bkm:Ref489953949 ), or a hortative, as in ( bkm:Ref489953950 ).

mwákùrítèèzà\\
mu-áku-rí-teez-a\\
sm 2 - sbjv. ipfv - refl -listen- fv \\
‘You have to listen to each other.’

ndákùmènèkàngà\\
ndi-áku-menek-ang-a\\
sm 1SG - sbjv. ipfv -wake_early- hab - fv \\
‘I should regularly wake up early.’ (NF_Elic17)

Like the perfective subjunctive, the imperfective subjunctive may combine with the adverb nanga ‘even’, not to express uncertainty, as is the case for the perfective subjunctive, but to express immediate future, as in ( bkm:Ref490842863 -- bkm:Ref99103420 ).

nàngà ndákàyà\\
nanga ndi-áka-y-a\\
even sm 1SG - sbjv. ipfv. dist -go- fv \\
‘I am about to leave.’ (NF_Elic15)

òmùndáré nàngà wákùbîzwà\\
o-mu-ndaré nanga u-áku-bízw-a\\
aug - np 3 -maize even sm 3 - sbjv. ipfv -ripen- fv \\
‘The maize is almost ripe/is about to ripen.’

nàngà bákùhùrà ndìkàréː ꜝbákànànúkà\\
nanga ba-áku-hur-a ndi-ka-réː bá̲-ka-nanuk-á̲\\
even sm 2 - sbjv. ipfv -arrive- fv cop - adv -long sm 2. rel - dist -leave- fv \\
‘S/he is about to arrive, s/he left a long time ago.’ (NF_Elic17)
summary:
The imperfective subjunctive is marked by the post-initial prefix áku-, and verbs in this form keep their underlying tones without any additional melodic high tones beyond the prefix itself. The text notes that its ku element likely comes from the infinitive prefix ku-, as suggested by alternations with distal marking and by its lack of melodic tones, which is typical of infinitives.

This form is often used with habitual meaning, especially with the habitual suffix -ang, though without -ang it can also be interpreted as progressive in some cases. It can also express command or hortative meanings, and with the adverb nanga ‘even’ it can indicate immediate future rather than uncertainty; a near-future imperfective can also be formed with the prefix mbo-.

text: In addition to tense and aspect, which situate an event in time, Fwe verbs may be inflected for space, situating the event in the physical space. The distal marker indicates that the event takes place away from the deictic center, e.g. in a place other than where the utterance is spoken ( bkm:Ref489965878 ). Fwe also has a locative pluractional, which indicates that an event takes place in multiple locations ( bkm:Ref494442567 ).
summary: Fwe verbs can be inflected not only for tense and aspect, which locate events in time, but also for space, which locates events physically. The distal marker shows that an event occurs away from the deictic center, such as somewhere other than the speech location, and Fwe also has a locative pluractional marker for events that take place in multiple locations.

text:
Fwe has a post-initial distal prefix ka -, not to be confused with the pre-initial prefix ka-, which marks the remote past imperfective (see bkm:Ref492377456 ), or negation (see bkm:Ref490843739 ). The prefix ka - as a distal marker is well-attested in Bantu languages, especially in south-central Bantu.

The distal is used to indicate that an action takes place away from the deictic center, usually the place where the utterance is spoken. In the utterance in ( bkm:Ref431991588 ), the speaker uses the distal because it is spoken at a place other than his house, hence the action referred to and the place where the utterance is spoken are not the same. The use of the distal in ( bkm:Ref431991716 ) is necessary because this utterance describes an action taking place in Namibia, and the utterance was spoken at the speaker’s home village in Zambia.

kùnjûò ndìkàzwâ\\
ku-N-júo ndi-ka-zw-á̲\\
np 17 - np 9 -house sm 1SG - dist -come_out- fv \\
‘I came from home.’ (NF_Elic15)

mwákàrí kwànàmíbyá kàndìkàsèbèzâ\\
mu-ákarí kwa-namibyá ka-ndi-ka-sebez-á̲\\
np 3 -last_year np 17 -Namibia pst. ipfv - sm 1SG - dist -work- fv \\
‘Last year I worked in Namibia.’ (ZF_Elic14)

Bantu languages with distal ka- may differ in terms of which moods the distal ka- can combine with. In Fwe, the distal ka- can be used in all moods. Examples of the distal marker used in the indicative were given in ( bkm:Ref431991588 ) and ( bkm:Ref431991716 ). The distal marker can also combine with an infinitive, as in ( bkm:Ref416186425 ). When the distal combines with an infinitive, the infinitive prefix ku- is replaced by the distal prefix ka-. The change from the infinitive prefix ku- to ka- when used with a distal is one of the main diagnostics that can be used to identify infinitives, both synchronically and diachronically, in verbal constructions that derive from earlier infinitive forms. The other main diagnostic is lack of melodic tone.

nàndámànà kàtémà èmìsùmò\\
na-ndí̲-a-man-a ka-tém-a e-mi-sumo\\
rem - sm 1SG - pst -finish- fv inf. dist -chop- fv aug - np 4 -pole\\
‘I finished chopping poles there.’ (ZF_Elic14)

The distal can also be used with verbs in the imperative, as in ( bkm:Ref451417267 -- bkm:Ref494982220 ), and in the subjunctive, as in ( bkm:Ref451417268 ). Note that the imperative and the subjunctive take the same form, but are distinguished by the use of the subject marker (see Chapter bkm:Ref99112450 ).

yêndè kàtêkè mênjì\\
é̲nd-e ka-té̲k-e ma-ínji\\
go- pfv. sbjv dist -fetch- pfv. sbjv np 6 -water\\
‘Go and fetch water.’ (ZF_Elic14)

kàsúmwínè bànyòkò\\
ka-sumwin-é̲ ba-nyoko\\
dist -tell- pfv. sbjv np 2 -mother\\
‘Go tell your mother.’ (NF_Elic17)

kùtêyè ndìkàkùmbùré rùkùmbà\\
kuteye ndi-ka-kumbur-é̲ ru-kumba\\
that sm 1SG - dist -strip- pfv. sbjv np 11 -fibre\\
‘… in order to cut strips of fibre there.’ (ZF_Narr14)

In many Bantu languages, the distal ka - is interpreted as ‘to go and X’. This itive semantics is possibly the result of a grammaticalization of a verb ‘to go’, for which evidence can be found in southern Bantoid and northwestern Narrow Bantu languages. The development of distal markers from verbs of motion is a well-attested grammaticalization path (: 103-104), and is also seen in two Tanzanian Bantu languages. The link between the distal marker and an itive interpretation is not seen in all languages, however; in Yeyi, a Bantu language geographically but not genealogically close to Fwe, the distal marker ka - is not interpreted as itive. In Fwe, itive semantics do appear to form a central part of the interpretation of the distal marker ka -. This is seen in the use of the distal with imperative verbs, as in example ( bkm:Ref494982220 ) above, where the itive semantics ‘go and’ is contributed by the distal marker alone. Another example showing that motion is a necessary component for the use of distal ka- is illustrated in ( bkm:Ref416188091 -- bkm:Ref74909097 ), drawn from a narrative. In ( bkm:Ref416188091 ), the speaker narrates that he moves away from the deictic center, as attested by his use of the distal marker ka- on the verb. Having reached this place, a second event takes place; he hears Claudia calling him. His hearing of Claudia takes place away from the deictic center, but no movement is involved; therefore, the distal marker is not used in ( bkm:Ref74909097 ).

àhá ndíkàhùrá kùrwâmbà\\
a-ha ndí̲-ka-hur-á̲ ku-ru-ámba\\
dem. i 16 sm 1SG. rel - dist -arrive- fv np 17 - np 11- middle_of_field\\
‘(…) when I reached the middle of the field…’

ndìshùwîrè bàklàùdìyà bàndìkûwà\\
ndi-shu H -í̲re ba-klaudia ba-ndi-kú̲-a\\
sm 1SG -hear- stat np 2 -Claudia sm 2 - om 1SG -call\\
‘I heard Mrs. Claudia calling me.’ (ZF_Narr13)

These examples suggest that motion is a necessary component of the interpretation of the distal prefix ka-. More specifically, it encodes motion away from the deictic center, and is not used for motion towards the deictic center. In ( bkm:Ref431992358 ), the verb bàhúrè ‘he will arrive’ is used without the distal because the place of the expected arrival is the same place as the place of speaking. In ( bkm:Ref431992424 ), the verb kàndíkêːzyà ‘I was coming’ is used without the distal because it describes a journey that ends at the place of speaking.

ênì òbùrótù mbòkúꜝté bàhúrè tùrâːrè\\
éni o-bu-rótu N-bo-kúteyé ba-hur-é̲ tu-rá̲ːr-e \\
yes aug - np 14 -good cop - np 14 -that sm 2 -arrive- pfv. sbjv
sm 1PL -sleep- pfv. sbjv \\
‘Yes, it’s good that he comes back and we spend the night here.’ (NF_Narr15)

àhá kàndíkêːzyà ndàhîtì òcècì\\
a-ha ka-ndí̲-ké̲ːzy-a ndi-a-hít-i o-∅-ceci\\
aug - dem. i 16 pst. ipfv - sm 1SG -come- fv
sm 1SG- pst -pass- npst. pfv aug - np 1a -church\\
‘When I came here, I passed by the church.’ (ZF_Elic14)
summary:
Fwe has a post-initial distal prefix ka-, distinct from a pre-initial ka- used for remote past imperfective or negation. This distal marks action away from the deictic center, can occur in all moods, and also appears with infinitives, imperatives, and subjunctives.

In Fwe, the distal often has itive meaning ‘go and X’, and this interpretation is tied to motion away from the deictic center. The prefix is not used for motion toward the deictic center or for events occurring at the speech location.

text:
The post-initial prefixes yabú- and kabú- both express a locative pluractional, an event that is carried out in different places. kabú - and yabú - are interchangeable, and no difference in meaning could be observed. Which form is used appears to depend on the individual speaker’s preference. Both locative pluractional prefixes are illustrated in ( bkm:Ref99103614 ).

cìkàbúkùkà cìyàbúkùkà\\
ci-kabú/yabú-kuk-a\\
sm 7 - loc. pl -float- fv \\
‘It floats, it goes by floating.’ (NF_Elic17)

The locative pluractional indicates an event taking place in different places: in ( bkm:Ref489874030 ), without locative pluractional, the verb rí ː zy indicates climbing in one place, and in ( bkm:Ref74909162 ), with a locative pluractional, the verb rí ː zy indicates climbing in several places.

ndìkwèsì ndìrî̲ːzyà\\
ndi-kwesi ndi-ríːzy-a\\
sm 1SG - prog sm 1SG -climb- fv \\
‘I am climbing.’

ndìkàbúrìːzyà\\
ndi-kabú-riːzy-a\\
sm 1SG - loc. pl -climb- fv \\
‘I am going around climbing, I am climbing in different places.’ (NF_Elic17)

The locative pluractional differs from the two other pluractional strategies used in Fwe, which are not strictly locative. As discussed in bkm:Ref489866362, these pluractional strategies may express that an event is repeated, or involves multiple participants. The locative pluractional suffix yabú -/ kabú- only expresses that an event is repeated in different locations. It may combine with either or both of the other pluractional strategies, as in ( bkm:Ref99103664 -- bkm:Ref99103665 ), combining the interpretation of event repetition of pluractional I or II with the locative pluractional’s interpretation of spatial distribution.

Locative pluractional + Pluractional I (suffix -a)\\
ndìkàbúbàsùndàíkà\\
ndi-kabú-ba-sund-a-ik-á̲\\
sm 1SG - loc. pl - om 2 -point- pl 1- imp. tr - fv \\
‘I am going around pointing at them.’

Locative pluractional + Pluractional II (stem reduplication)\\
àkàbúkàbìràkàbìrà múmàràpá ꜝábàntù\\
a-kabú-kabira-kabir-a mú-ma-rapá a-á=ba-ntu\\
sm 1 - loc. pl - pl 2-enter- fv np 18 - np 6 -courtyard pp 6 - con = np 2 -person\\
‘S/he keeps going round entering people's courtyards.’ (NF_Elic17)

Locative pluractional + Pluractional I + Pluractional II\\
nàkàyâ ìyé àkábúyèndàùràyèndàùrà òkábúbônà\\
na=ka-y-á iyé a-kabú-endaura-end-a-ur-a o-kabú-bón-a \\
com = inf. dist -go- fv that
sm 1 - loc. pl - pl 2-go- pl 1- sep. tr - fv aug - loc. pl -see- fv \\
‘And he went out to walk around, and look around.’ (NF_Narr17)

The exact interpretation of the locative pluractional depends on the lexical aspect of the verb, as well as the wider linguistic context. Two main interpretations are possible: associated motion, where the event and motion co-occur (‘go while X-ing’), and distributive, where the event alternates with motion (‘go and X, go and X’). The associated motion interpretation of the locative pluractional is available with verbs that have a long nucleus, such as dynamic verbs. This is illustrated with the verb shíb ‘whistle’ in ( bkm:Ref99103717 ), which expresses whistling while moving when combined with the locative pluractional.

àkábúꜝshíbà\\
a-kabú-shib-á̲\\
sm 1 - loc. pl -whistle- fv \\
‘S/he whistles while walking.’ (NF_Elic17)

Stative verbs also have a long nucleus, and therefore the locative pluractional is interpreted as associated motion with these verbs, as shown for the stative verb tíy ‘be afraid’ in ( bkm:Ref497245742 ).

àkàbútìyà\\
a-kabú-tiy-a\\
sm 1 - loc. pl -be_afraid- fv \\
‘S/he is afraid on the way/while going.’ (NF_Elic17)

The locative pluractional may also take a distributive interpretation with dynamic verbs, marking that an event takes place in different places, as in ( bkm:Ref99103790 ).

mbùryàhó kàbákàbúpàngà bùryáhò\\
N-bu-ryahó ka-bá̲-kabú-pang-a bu-ryahó\\
cop - np 14 -like_that pst. ipfv - sm 2 - loc. pl -do- fv np 14 -like_that\\
‘That is how he used to do in different places.’ (NF_Narr17)

Whether the locative pluractional with dynamic verbs is interpreted as associated motion or distributive depends on the lexical semantics of the verb, as well as the wider context. The associated motion interpretation is typically limited to events that may logically co-occur with motion, such as motion verbs, as in ( bkm:Ref99103820 -- bkm:Ref99103822 ).

ndìyàbúyèndà bùryáhò ndókùryàt’ énjôkà\\

The locative pluractional has a distributive interpretation with change-of-state verbs that lack an onset phase, such as the verb w ‘fall’ in ( bkm:Ref497245841 ); when combined with the locative pluractional, it expresses something that repeatedly falls in different places.

‘It keeps falling. (while traveling; the item keeps falling out of your pocket in different places)’ (NF_Elic17)

summary:
The post-initial prefixes yabú- and kabú- are interchangeable locative pluractionals in Fwe, with no observed difference in meaning and speaker preference determining which form is used. They indicate that an event is carried out in different places, but their interpretation depends on the verb and context, yielding either associated motion (“go while X-ing”) or distributive readings (“go and X, go and X”), and they can combine with other pluractional strategies.

With dynamic verbs, the locative pluractional can mark repeated action in different locations or motion accompanied by the action, while with certain change-of-state verbs it can indicate repeated falling in different places or a gradual change over time. The passage also notes that with verbs like “get rich,” “become heavy,” and “become hot,” yabú-/kabú- expresses gradual development.

text:
The markers kabú - and yabú- are historically derived from an inflected verb followed by a verb with the adverbial prefix bú- (see bkm:Ref489870394 on adverbs). The syllable ya is derived from the lexical verb ya ‘go’, which is still used in Fwe with this meaning. kabú- is the result of the contraction of distal ka- with the locative pluractional yabú-. In modern Fwe, ka-yabú- is considered to be interchangeable with kabú-, as shown in ( bkm:Ref99103952 ). The original deictic semantics of distal ka- have been lost in kabú-, which does not mark motion away from the deictic center.

ùkàyàbútùmbúkà ùkàbútùmbúkà\\
u-ka-yabú-tumbuk-á u-kabú-tumbuk-á\\
sm 3 - dist - loc. pl -burn- fv sm 3 - loc. pl -burn- fv \\
‘It [fire] comes while burning.’ (NF_Elic17)

When the prefix yabú -/ kabú- grammaticalized, the earlier inflected verb lost its status as an independent lexical verb. This can be seen by the lack of melodic tone in the ya / ka element, and by optional high tone spread from bú to the preceding syllable, e.g. yábú- and kábú-. High tone spread does not cross word boundaries (see bkm:Ref430865664 ), so its occurrence shows that the formerly independent verb has become part of the prefix.

A similar marker yabo- is found in Subiya, as in ch’o ya bo sibila ‘he goes while whistling’, which is also analyzed as a combination of the prefix bo and the lexical verb ya ‘go’.
summary:
The markers **kabú-** and **yabú-** are historically derived from a combination of an inflected verb and a verb with the adverbial prefix **bú-**, with **ya** coming from the lexical verb meaning “go.” In modern Fwe, **ka-yabú-** and **kabú-** are interchangeable, and the original deictic meaning of distal **ka-** has been lost, so **kabú-** no longer marks motion away from the deictic center.

The passage also argues that **yabú-/kabú-** has grammaticalized into a prefix, since the earlier verb no longer behaves like an independent lexical verb and tonal patterns show it has become part of the prefix. A similar construction, **yabo-**, is reported in Subiya and analyzed in the same way.
